title: Course information
text:
In this course, we are going to study the linear regression model and we use two different sources for this. Magnus (2017) studies the multiple linear regression model using vector and matrix notation. The contents of this website instead focus on the simple linear regression model using unit-specific notation. The case with only one explanatory variable is important to understand regression models in more detail. Moreover, it highlights the usefulness of analyzing models, estimators and tests using different types of notations. These are very important skils for an econometrician.






Tip📚 Literature




Magnus, J.R. (2017). Introduction to the Theory of Econometrics. Sixth printing onwards. VU University Press.
The contents of this website.



The course is mostly theoretical of nature but also considers empirical aspects of econometric modelling. In period 1, we focus on the following main topics:

Estimation: how can we estimate the parameters in the model and what are the properties of these estimators?
The fit: even if we are able to estimate the parameters, we still do not know how well the model fits the data.
Prediction: based on our estimated model, how can we predict the dependent variable if we have values for the independent variables?
Inference: we want to be able to test hypotheses, construct confidence and prediction intervals.

In period 2, we dig a bit deeper and consider three themes:

Estimation: a new estimation method (maximum likelihood), adapting an existing estimation technique (weighted least sqauares) and estimation under restrictions.
Asymptotics: we study the properties of our estimators for sample size going to infinity. The latter never happens in practice, but it provides a good approximation of the sampling distribution in case of a large number of observations. Moreover, we can use the results for hypothesis testing.
Assumptions: how can we check or test whether the assumptions underlying the linear regression model hold true? We consider functional misspecification, multicollinearity, non-normality and heteroskedasticity. We give extra attention to the last topic and discuss remedies, because it often occurs in applications.

title: Week 6 - Conditioning
text:
This week’s contents
So far, we covered Chapter 1 to 3 in ITE. We derived the estimators \(\widehat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\), \(s^{2} = e'e/(n-k)\) under the condition that they are unbiased. We continued by deriving test statistics for single and multiple linear restrictions. These results were found based on the classical assumptions for the linear regression model, except for one. The assumption that \(X\) is nonrandom has been motivated in Section 2.7 using the argument that the basics of econometric theory do not change if we make this simplifying assumption. Whereas this is true, any good econometrician needs to know how to deal with conditioning, which is the title of this week’s Chapter 6. Since you are already familiar with this topic from your previous probability theory and statistics course, we will focus almost exclusively on the linear regression model. We revisit some of the previously found results and see how their derivation changes when \(X\) is assumed random.






Tip📚 Read in ITE




Section 6.1 - 6.4. These sections intuitively explain the concept of conditioning and help you refresh your memory on the concept.
Section 6.5. This section introduces two very important concepts: the law of total expectation (also called the law of iterated expectations or the tower property) and the law of total variance.

title: Week 6 - Conditioning
text:
The simple linear regression model
Consider the simple linear regression model \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}, \qquad (i = 1,\ldots, n),
\] where \(x_{i}\) is assumed to be random. This means that \(u_{i}\) is no longer the only random part on the right-hand side of this equation and thus we need to make an assumption about the relationship between \(u_{i}\) and \(x_{i}\).
An often chosen assumption is mean-independence, which can be expressed as \(E(u_{i}|x_{i}) = 0\), because it is stronger than uncorrelatedness between \(u_{i}\) and \(x_{i}\) and weaker than independence (which is deemed unrealistic). This condition is also called strict exogeneity. In addition, variance-independence is imposed, which shows that the variance of \(u_{i}\) does not depend on \(x_{i}\), i.e. \(\Var(u_{i}|x_{i}) = \sigma^{2}\). This is called homoskedasticity and we study its implications in more detail in the second part of this course.
These assumptions give a clear interpretation to the linear regression. Note that \[
\begin{aligned}
E(y_{i}|x_{i}) &= E(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i} | x_{i}) \\
               &= \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}E(x_{i}|x_{i}) + E(u_{i} | x_{i}) \\
               &= \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i},
\end{aligned}
\] because \(E(u_{i}|x_{i}) = 0\) by strict exogeneity. Thus, the population linear regression line simply represents the conditional mean of \(y_{i}\) given \(x_{i}\). This also reveals how to proceed in terms of prediction. In that case, we need the sample linear regression line which then represents an estimate of the conditional mean of \(y_{i}\) given \(x_{i}\).
We may also compute the conditional variance of \(y_{i}\) given \(x_{i}\). Note that \[
\Var(y_{i} | x_{i}) = \Var(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i} | x_{i}) = \Var(u_{i}|x_{i}) = \sigma^{2},
\] since the systemic part \(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i}\) is fixed conditional on \(x_{i}\). The difference with the unconditional variance of \(y_{i}\) is important to notice. Using the law of total variance: \[
\begin{aligned}
E(y_{i}) &= E(\Var(y_{i}|x_{i})) + \Var(E(y_{i}|x_{i})) \\
         &= E(\sigma^{2}) + \Var(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i}) \\
         &= \sigma^{2} + \beta_{2}^{2}\Var(x_{i}) \\
         &= \sigma^{2} + \beta_{2}^{2}\sigma^{2}_{x},
\end{aligned}
\] which has the nice interpretation that the total variation in \(y_{i}\) is the sum of variation explained by \(x_{i}\) and the unexplained variation from \(u_{i}\). So, even though the variance of \(y_{i}\) conditional on \(x_{i}\) is always \(\sigma^{2}\), the unconditional variance also contains variation arising because \(x_{i}\) itself varies across observations.

Unbiasedness of the least-squares estimator
Because \(x_{i}\) is now random, the least-squares estimators \(\widehat{\beta}_{1}\), \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\) and \(s^{2} = \frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{u}_{i}^{2}\) are now highly nonlinear functions of \((y, X)\). Under the conditions that we just imposed, we can still show unbiasedness of these estimators. Let’s focus on \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\).
Under correct specification, i.e. the model and DGP coincide,note that we can write \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}},
\] which we already showed in Week 2.






NoteReminder





Note that \[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\beta}_{2} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i} - (\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}\overline{x} + \overline{u}))}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(\beta_{2}(x_{i} - \overline{x}) + (u_{i} - \overline{u}))}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(u_{i} - \overline{u})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\] Note that we plugged in the DGP at the second equality, the third and fourth equalities are rearranging terms, and the last equality follows from \(\overline{u}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x}) = 0\).



Taking expectations now yields \[
\begin{aligned}
E(\widehat{\beta}_{2}) &= E\left[ \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \right] \\
&= E(\beta_{2}) + E \left[ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}  \right] \\
&= \beta_{2} + E \left[ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}  \right].
\end{aligned}
\] To obtain the desired result \(E(\widehat{\beta}_{2}) = \beta_{2}\), we need to show that this second term equals zero. We are going to use the law of total expectations, because the term involves several random variables. If we define \(X = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})\), we can proceed as follows: \[
\begin{aligned}
E \left( \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}  \right) &=
E_{X} \left( \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})E_{u_{i}|X}(u_{i}| X)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}  \right) \\
&= E_{X} \left( \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x}) \cdot 0}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}  \right)
= 0,
\end{aligned}
\] where some subtle steps need extra explanation:

The first equality makes use of the law of total expectations. We have to condition on \(X = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})\) and not just a single \(x_{i}\), otherwise we may not take \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})\) outside of the inner expectation.
The inner expectation is taken with respect to the conditional distribution \(u_{i} | x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\), while the outer expectation is with respect to \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\). To emphasize with respect to what distribution we take the expectation, we included them as subscripts. You may do this as well, but note that it is not mandatory.
By combining \(\Cov(u_{i}, u_{j}) = 0\) for all \(i \neq j\) and normality, we have independence of all pairs of observations \((x_{i}, y_{i})\) and \((x_{j}, y_{j})\) for all \(i \neq j\). Therefore, we can conclude \(E_{u_{i}|X}(u_{i} | X) = E_{u_{i}|X}(u_{i} | x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}) = E_{u_{i}|x_{i}}(u_{i} | x_{i}) = 0\).

We have now calculated the unconditional expectation of \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\), which shows that the estimator is indeed unbiased. For completeness, we can also compute its variance. Let us first compute the conditional variance: \[
\begin{aligned}
\Var(\widehat{\beta}_{2} | X) &= \Var\left( \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \Bigg| X \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{[\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}]^{2}} \Var\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i} | X \right) \\
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}{[\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}]^{2}} \Var(u_{i} | X ) \\
&= \frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\] We are now ready to compute the unconditional variance using the law of total variance.: \[
\begin{aligned}
\Var(\widehat{\beta}_{2}) &= E(\Var(\widehat{\beta}_{2} | X)) + \Var(E(\widehat{\beta}_{2}|X)) \\
&= E\left( \frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \right) + \Var(\beta_{2}) \\
&= \sigma^{2} E\left(\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Empirical applications
The past weeks’ main focus has been on the theory behind the multiple linear regression model. We have looked at the ideal conditions, derived estimators and their corresponding standard errors as well as confidence intervals, prediction (intervals) and studied how to perform tests for single and multiple linear restrictions on the vector \(\beta\). We have even touched upon the topics model selection and model averaging.
This puts us in a position to apply the model to real data and to correctly interpret its results. Running these analyses yourself will be addressed in the second part of the course, but let us consider two empirical applications from the book Mastering Econometrics.






NoteThe relationship between price and sales

We could answer these questions as follows:

The regression line suggests a negative relationship between price and sales. There are about 21 sales at a price of 50 euros, about 18 at a price of 100 euros, and about 15 at a price of 150 euros. Formally, a unit increase in price leads to a decrease of about 0.066 in sales. The relationship is statistically significant at the conventional \(5\%\) and \(1\%\) significance levels \(\alpha\), which can be verified by comparing the \(t\)-statistic with the \((\alpha/2)\)-quantiles (for two-sided tests) of the Student \(t\)-distribution with 418 degrees of freedom. In practice, we use the normal approximation when the degrees of freedom exceeds \(30\). Since we know that \(\Pr(|z|<1.96)=0.95\) and \(\Pr(|z|<2.57)=0.99\) when \(z \sim N(0,1)\), and both \(36.730\) and \(11.750\) are well above 1.96 and 2.57, the two estimates are significant.
The \(95\%\) confidence interval is given by \[
(\hat\beta_{2} - 1.96\sqrt{s^{2}v_{22}},\; \hat\beta_{2} + 1.96\sqrt{s^{2}v_{22}})
= (-0.078, -0.054),
\] where the standard error \(\sqrt{s^{2}v_{22}}\) equals \(0.006\). Thus, \(\beta_{2} = 0\) is not included in the \(95\%\) confidence interval, in agreement with the significance of the estimate discussed under (a).
For a price \(x_{*} = 80\), the prediction is \(\hat{y}_{*} = \hat{\beta}_{1} + \hat{\beta}_{2} \times 80 = 19.114\), and for \(x_{*} = 300\), the prediction is \(19.114\). The second prediction is less reliable because we have only a few observations for such large prices.
One of the limitations of a linear approximation is that it may not be a good approximation when we move away from the center. For example, sales cannot be negative, and a linear model would lead to negative sales whenever the price is (very) large. This does not mean that the model is useless, but it only provides a useful approximation for prices between, say, 30 and 200.




The previous empirical application makes use of the simple linear regression model, which is very popular due to its straightforward interpretation and ability to clearly visualize the results. However, a regression model with only one independent variable is often insufficient to capture the essence of the problem. If we regress sales on price, then we explicitly allow sales to only depend on that single factor. It is very likely that sales are also explained by other factors than price, such as the type of shoes, the material of the shoes, the friendliness of the salesperson, et cetera. These variables are currently absorbed in the error term, and they may be correlated with price. Because of this, we may systematically over- or underestimate \(\beta_{2}\). This argument is made clearly in Section 3.8 of ITE: we might include other regressors (auxiliary variables) simply to get a reliable estimate of the coefficient related to our focus variable (i.e., price in this case). This is the case for \(\log Q\) and \(\log p_F\), and also (but marginally) for the constant term. The null hypothesis states that all coefficients, except for the intercept, are equal to zero. This test is sometimes called the test of overall significance, and it tests whether the intercept-only model fits the data as well as our proposed regression model. In our case, the value of the \(F\)-statistic is 14.585, which is higher than the critical value of the \(F(4,140)\)-distribution, which is 2.436. Thus, we reject the null hypothesis. title: Week 4 - Inference
text:
This week’s contents
So far, we have focused on estimation of \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^{2}\), model fit and making predictions in the linear regression model. Last week ended with considerations regarding model selection, in which the bias-variance trade-off played a central role.
This week, we study another important topic: inference. We start with hypothesis testing and study meticulously what ingredients are necessary to have a valid test statistic. We first need to derive the exact distributions of \(\widehat{\beta}\) and \(s^{2}\), and establish the independence of these two estimators. Based on this, we can establish the \(t\)-ratio. We revisit statistical concepts that you are already familiar with, such as the null hypothesis, maintained hypothesis, the \(p\)-value and the signficance level of a test. We discuss two main applications of the \(t\)-ratio: testing a hypothesis of interest and diagnostic testing. We end the week by considering the size and the power of a test.

title: Week 4 - Inference
section: Hypothesis testing in the linear regression model
text:
Hypothesis testing in the linear regression model
Let us first consider the simple linear regression model \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}.
\tag{1}\] Suppose there is a company that has \(n\) different stores located in Amsterdam. It wants to use this model to evaluate the effectiveness of the promotion activities of these stores. Let \(x_{i}\) be the amount of money spent on advertisements by store \(i\) and let \(y_{i}\) denote the sales of store \(i\). The company has three managers, the one more optimistic than the other, and they ask the following questions:

Did the promotion activities have an effect on the sales at all?
Did the promotion activities translate at least into a one-to-one increase in sales?
Did we manage to get twice the amount of sales out of our promotion activities, or was it less?

If you were to work for this company as an econometrician, you would have to translate these questions into statements that you can statistically test. We can do this by performing hypothesis tests on \(\beta_{2}\). In case of the first manager, the set of hypotheses is given by \[
H_{0}: \beta_{2} = 0 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_{1}: \beta_{2} \neq 0,
\] where the null hypothesis states that the money spent on promotion has no effect on the sales, while the alternative hypothesis states that it does have an effect. However, it leaves unspecified whether it is positive or negative, because it is a two-sided test. The second manager is a bit more positive, and wants to know whether the money spent is at least earned back through sales. This set of hypotheses can be formalized as \[
H_{0}: \beta_{2} = 1 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_{1}: \beta_{2} > 1,
\] where the null hypothesis states that a unit increase in \(x_{i}\) results in the same unit increase in \(y_{i}\). Because the manager specified `at least’ in the question, the alternative hypothesis considers the scenario that a single Euro spent on promotion leads to more than one Euro in sales, making this a one-sided test. As we will see, the alternative considers the right tail of the distribution. Finally, we have the most optimistic manager, whose set of hypotheses can be written as \[
H_{0}: \beta_{2} = 2 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_{1}: \beta_{2} < 2,
\] which is once again a one-sided test but concerns the left tail of the distribution.
To answer the questions posed by the managers, we need a testing procedure. Since the null hypotheses represent single (linear) restrictions, we can make use of a \(t\)-test. Let us first consider what is needed to have a valid test statistic.

title: Week 4 - Inference
text:
Student’s \(t\)-distribution
Before we derive the formal test statistic, let us first investigate how we can construct random variables with a Student’s \(t\)-distribution. Following Appendix B.4., and in particular Equation B.7, we can see that if \(x \sim N(0,1)\) (i.e., univariate standard normal) and \(w \sim \chi^{2}(n)\), and \(x\) and \(w\) independent, then \[
\frac{x}{\sqrt{w/n}} \sim t(n),
\tag{2}\] i.e., the ratio follows a Student’s \(t\)-distribution with \(n\) degrees of freedom. This result will prove useful whenever we want to perform tests of individual coefficients in the linear regression model.

title: Week 4 - Inference
section: Deriving the distributions of our estimators
text:
Deriving the distributions of our estimators
Let us now consider the multiple linear regression again to derive the distributions of \(\widehat{\beta}\), \(e\) and \(s^2\). This derivation could also be done using the simple linear regression model, but it is typically more convenient to immediately derive the formulas based on the multiple linear regression model.

Distribution of \(\widehat{\beta}\)
This week, we make extensive use of Assumption 2.4, which states that \(u \sim N(0,\sigma^{2}I_{n})\). In combination with Assumption 2.3 (\(X\) is nonrandom), this can also be written as \(y \sim N(X\beta,\sigma^{2}I_{n})\). We can now make use of an extremely useful property of the normal distribution. Since \(y\) is normally distributed and \(\widehat{\beta}\) is linear in \(y\), we obtain \[
\widehat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y \sim N(\beta, \sigma^{2}(X'X)^{-1}).
\]






NoteMean and variance of \(\hat{\beta}\)





Using Section B.1, we can find the mean and variance of \(\hat{\beta}\) as follows. For the mean, we obtain \[
E(\widehat{\beta}) = E((X'X)^{-1}X'y) = (X'X)^{-1}X'E(y) = (X'X)^{-1}X'X\beta = \beta,
\] while the variance is given by \[
\begin{aligned}
\Var(\widehat{\beta}) &= \Var((X'X)^{-1}X'y) \\
&= (X'X)^{-1}X'\Var(y)X(X'X)^{-1} \\
&= (X'X)^{-1}X'\sigma^{2}I_{n}X(X'X)^{-1} \\
&= \sigma^{2}(X'X)^{-1},
\end{aligned}
\] where we used that \(\sigma^{2}\) is a scalar, \(X\) is nonrandom and \(X'X\) is invertible because \(X\) has full rank by Assumption 2.2.





Distribution of \(e\)
For the residuals, we have seen that they are also linear in \(y\) and even \(u\) since \(e = My = Mu\). It is straightforward to derive \(E(e) = ME(u) = 0\) and \(\Var(e) = \Var(Mu) = M\Var(u)M' = \sigma^{2}M\), where we use that \(M\) is symmetric and idempotent. There is, however, one important difference. As we have seen before, the variance matrix of \(e\) does not have full rank (we also call this rank-deficient). Because \(M\) is singular, the distribution of \(e\) is degenerate. Intuitively, this means that the \(n \times 1\) random vector \(e\) has a support (the space where all the probability mass lives) that lies entirely within a subspace of dimension strictly less than \(n\).






NoteReminder





Because \(M\) is symmetric and idempotent, we can calculate its rank using the trace: \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{tr}(M) &= \text{tr}(I_{n} - X(X'X)^{-1}X') \\
             &= \text{tr}(I_{n}) - \text{tr}(X(X'X)^{-1}X') \\
             &= \text{tr}(I_{n}) - \text{tr}(X'X(X'X)^{-1}) \\
             &= \text{tr}(I_{n}) - \text{tr}(I_{k}) \\
             &= n - k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\Var(e) = \sigma^{2}M\), we know that the support of the \(n \times 1\) random vector \(e\) lies within a subspace of dimension \(n-k\). This is due to the fact that least squares imposes \(k\) first-order conditions.





Distribution of \(s^2\)
We now have the main ingredients to derive the distribution of \(s^{2}\), but need to rely on Appendix B.4 once more. We make use of the following result given in Equation B.6: if \(x \sim N(0, I_{n})\) and \(A\) is a symmetric idempotent matrix of rank \(r\), then \(x'Ax \sim \chi^{2}(r)\). Let us apply this result to find the distribution of \(s^{2} = e'e/(n-k)\).
Note that \(e'e = (Mu)'Mu = u'Mu\) because \(M\) is symmetric and idempotent. We know that \(u \sim N(0,\sigma^{2}I_{n})\) such that \(v = u/\sigma \sim N(0,I_{n})\) and that \(\text{r}(M) = n-k\). Then applying Equation B.6 to these quantities gives \[
\frac{e'e}{\sigma^{2}} = v'Mv \sim \chi^{2}(n-k).
\] Using \(s^{2} = e'e/(n-k)\) we obtain \[
\frac{(n-k)s^{2}}{\sigma^{2}} \sim \chi^{2}(n-k).
\] Using the information about the \(\chi^{2}\)-distribution, we can easily derive the mean and variance of \(s^{2}\) but we won’t do that here because it is not crucial to derive the \(t\)-test.


Independence between \(\widehat{\beta}\) and \(s^2\)
If we plug \(y = X\beta + u\) into our least-squares estimator \(\widehat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\) and rearrange terms, we obtain \[
\widehat{\beta} - \beta = (X'X)^{-1}X'u = \sigma(X'X)^{-1}X'v,
\] which is a linear form given by \(\sigma Lv\) by defining \(L = (X'X)^{-1}X'\). Moreover, we can write \[
e'e = u'Mu = \sigma^{2}v'Mv,
\] which is a quadratic form in terms of \(v\). Since \(LM = 0\) (as \(MX = 0\)), we now know by Equation B.9 in Appendix B.5, that \(Lv\) and \(v'Mv\) are independent. This is sufficient to show that \(\widehat{\beta}\) and \(s^{2}\) are independent.

title: Week 4 - Inference
text:
Constructing the \(t\)-ratio
Note that we are now almost in the position to apply (2). Let us first have a closer look at \(\widehat{\beta}\), for which we derived \(\widehat{\beta} \sim N(\beta, \sigma^{2}(X'X)^{-1})\). If we define \(V = (X'X)^{-1}\), then we have \(\widehat{\beta}_{j} \sim N(\beta_{j}, \sigma^{2}v_{jj})\) for the \(j\)th element in the random vector \(\widehat{\beta}\). In other words, \[
\frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j} - \beta_{j}}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}v_{jj}}} \sim N(0,1).
\tag{3}\]






NoteWhy not use this result for testing?





If \(\sigma^{2}\) is known, then (3) could be used for testing. For example, since \[
\Pr\left( -1.96 < \frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j} - \beta_{j}}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}v_{jj}}} < 1.96 \right) = 0.95,
\] we can test two-sided at a \(5\%\) significance level. If the value of \(\frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j} - \beta_{j}}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}v_{jj}}}\) lies inside the interval \((-1.96, 1.96)\) we fail to reject \(H_{0}\), while we reject \(H_{0}\) if the computed value falls outside the interval.
Unfortunately, we typically cannot use this result for testing because \(\sigma^{2}\) is generally unknown.



Because the previous result cannot be used for testing, we have to find another solution. We cannot “simply replace” \(\sigma^{2}\) by its estimator \(s^{2}\) without any justification, but we can apply (2). Note that applying this result will have exactly the outcome that we hinted at (replace \(\sigma^{2}\) by \(s^{2}\)) but the distribution of this new statistic changes:
\[
\frac{(\widehat{\beta}_{j} - \beta_{j})/ \sqrt{\sigma^{2}v_{jj}}}{\sqrt{\frac{(n-k)s^{2}}{\sigma^{2}} / (n-k)}} = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j} - \beta_{j}}{\sqrt{s^{2}v_{jj}}} \sim t(n-k),
\tag{4}\] which is a feasible test statistic because all its elements can be computed. You might disagree with this statement, because the true \(\beta_{j}\) is typically also unknown. However, \(\beta_{j}\) plays a different role in this statistic: we may also call it the hypothesized value. Quite often we consider \(\beta_{j} = 0\), which provides the \(t\)-ratio. However, as the example with the three managers highlights, we may also be interested in other hypothesized values. We can use (4) to test the null hypotheses of these managers.

title: Week 4 - Inference
text:
Two interpretations of the \(t\)-ratio
At the start of this week’s page, we started off with the simple linear regression model in (1). As we already established, the hypotheses of the different managers involved performing tests on the slope coefficient \(\beta_{2}\). This is the first use of the \(t\)-ratio: we are interested in a clear (research) hypothesis which investigates the behavior of a focus variable on the dependent variable.
The simple linear regression model has some advantages, such as its easy interpretation and the ability to visually represent the results. The disadvantages are also substantial, though. If we revisit the empirical application where \(x_{i}\) represents the amount of money spent on promotion and \(y_{i}\) the sales, then we can draw an important conclusion. In this model, only the promotion is allowed to influence sales but this is arguably too simplistic. Sales are likely also influenced by other factors, such as the exact location of the store (in a busy shopping area or not), the size of the store (larger stores probably sell more), the (average) number of visitors in each store, et cetera. Because all these factors are not contained in the model, they are contained in the error term \(u_{i}\). In case one or more of these factors are correlated with \(x_{i}\), \(\beta_{2}\) is not correctly representing the effect of \(x_{i}\) on \(y_{i}\).
This is one of the main reasons why we study the multiple linear regression model. We might still only be interested in the effect of promotion on sales, but in order to get a better estimate of that effect, we include more regressors: \[
y = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \ldots + \beta_{k} x_{k} + u \quad \text{or in short,} \quad y = X\beta + u,
\tag{5}\] where \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}\) now represent \(k\) different regressors in vector form (not \(k\) observations on one regressor!). This brings about a second use of the \(t\)-ratio. For some regressors, we are not really interested in their direct effect of the dependent variable. They are called auxiliary or control variables. Performing tests on the coefficients corresponding to these variables is often also called diagnostic testing. This name reveals that the test is executed to assess the adequacy of the model rather than testing a (research) hypothesis of interest. If we consider 5 in terms of our empirical application:

If \(x_{2}\) represents promotion, then this variable is a focus variable. We can test our hypothesis of interest on \(\beta_{2}\).
This makes \(x_{3}, \ldots, x_{k}\) auxiliary variables, who are included to ensure a proper estimation of \(\beta_{2}\). If we perform tests on the remaining coefficients \(\beta_{3}, \ldots, \beta_{k}\), we typically refer to this as diagnostic testing.

Note that it is possible to have more than one focus variable. In what follows, we may choose to partition the design matrix \(X\) as follows \(X = (X_{1} : X_{2})\), where \(X_{1}\) are \(k_{1}\) focus variables and \(X_{2}\) are \(k_{2}\) auxiliary variables. We come back to this in the context of model selection.

title: Week 4 - Inference
text:
Size and power
The ability to perform statistical tests is an important tool for econometricians. However, it is important to be aware of the two errors that can be made during hypothesis testing. That is, (i) we may reject the null hypothesis while it is true (type I) or (ii) we may not reject the null hypothesis while it is false (type II). For a fixed sample size, the investigator must find a balance between these errors. The associated probabilities are defined by \[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &= \Pr(\text{reject } H_{0} | H_{0} \text{ is true}), \\
\beta  &= \Pr(\text{do not reject } H_{0} | H_{1} \text{ is true}).
\end{aligned}
\] These two quantities play a crucial role in testing. We recognize \(\alpha\) as the significance level that we set beforehand ourselves (in econometrics, we often choose \(\alpha = 0.05\)). In terms of testing, we also refer to the size of a test: we do not want the probability of making a Type I error to exceed the value of \(0.05\). Another important quantity is the power of a test, which is defined as \(1 - \beta\). Further elaboration on these concepts can be found in the last section of this week.






NoteAn example in the justice system





An effective way to think about hypothesis testing is to consider the saying innocent until proven guilty. Suppose a person got arrested suspected of murder. The saying indicates that our \(H_{0}\) is that the person is innocent. We only want to convict persons in case there is substantial evidence showing that they are indeed guilty.
In terms of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), we can say the following. Suppose the null hypothesis is true (the person is in fact innocent), then we want to make \(\alpha\) very small: we do not want an innocent person to go behind bars. We probably want to set \(\alpha\) smaller than the \(0.05\) that we typically choose in econometrics, because wrongfully sending people to jail in 5% of the cases is unacceptable (if this were a repeated experiment). However, a small significance level has adverse effects on the power of the test. That is, if the alternative is true (the person is in fact guilty), then the probability of actually rejecting \(H_{0}\) decreases. The murderer has a larger chance of going free.
The only way to reduce both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is to increase the number of observations. In the case at hand, to increase the pieces of evidence related to the murder scene.
As you can see, hypothesis testing takes a rather conservative view. In many cases, the null hypothesis says that there is “no effect” or in this example, “the person is innocent”. This means that we assume \(H_{0}\) to be true as long as we do not collect enough evidence against this null hypothesis.
Imagine now that we would do it the other way around. We would assume the person is guilty and the only way to clear the person’s name is whenever enough evidence is collected that shows innocence. If we took that point of view, probably many more people would end up behind bars (innocent or not)…

title: Week 2 - The linear regression model
text:
Contents
This week, we are going to move from approximation to estimation. We no longer assume that the world is nonrandom, but instead suppose that the data at our disposal are realizations of random variables. You might have the feeling that not much is changing, but we will spend some extra time highlighting the difference when we get to best unbiased estimation. But before discussing that, we are going to define the linear regression model, the corresponding terminology and a set of ideal conditions (assumptions). Moreover, we consider the important difference between a data-generation process (DGP) and a model. Lastly, we make a start with best unbiased estimation, which boils down to solving a restricted optimization problem.

title: Week 2 - The linear regression model
text:
The simple linear regression model
The simple linear regression model looks exactly the same as in the approximation framework \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}, \qquad (i=1, \ldots, n),
\] but its interpretation is quite different. In the previous setup, all observations \((x_{i}, y_{i})\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) were fixed. Thus, they could just be treated as given. The task was then simple: find the best-fitting line based on the criterion that the sum of squared distances from the line to the observations is as small as possible. However, we are now going to assume that \(y_{i}\) is a random variable called the dependent variable (or explained variable, regressand). This variable is related to an explanatory variable \(x_{i}\) (or independent variable, regressor). At first, we are going to assume that \(x_{i}\) is nonrandom. The basics of econometric theory do not change if we make this simplifying assumption and the material is easier to grasp. We call \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) the unknown parameters or coefficients of the model, and \(u_{i}\) the error term or disturbance term.






ImportantThe least-squares approximator



Last week, we derived the least-squares approximator in the non-random context. It turns out that the expression \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\) will also be the least-squares estimator. You might be under the impression that this is ‘obvious’, but it is actually far from! When we discuss best unbiased estimation, it will become clear that we will get to the same expression but by solving a completely different optimization problem!
Note that we will typically write “hats” on the coefficients to indicate estimators. For example, the least-squares estimator of \(\beta\) is denoted \(\widehat{\beta}\) (and no longer \(b\)).


Important to remember: \(y_{i}\) and \(u_{i}\) are random variables, \(x_{i}\), \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) are nonrandom. The variables \(y_{i}\) and \(x_{i}\) are observable, while \(\beta_{1}\), \(\beta_{2}\) and \(u_{i}\) are unobservable. The generalization to the multiple linear regression model can be found in ITE. We also study the ideal conditions (assumptions).

title: Week 2 - The linear regression model
text:
The role of assumptions
The assumptions introduced in ITE for the general model \[
y = X\beta + u,
\] are given by

Assumption 1: The model is linear.
Assumption 2: The \(n \times k\) matrix \(X\) is nonrandom and has rank \(k\).
Assumption 3: The \(n \times 1\) vector \(u\) has mean zero and variance \(\sigma^{2}I_{n}\).
Assumption 4: The \(n \times 1\) vector \(u\) follows a multivariate normal distribution.
Assumption 5: If we let \(Q_{n} = X'X/n\), then \(Q_{n} \to Q\) as \(n \to \infty\), where \(Q\) is a finite and positive definite \(k \times k\) matrix.

These assumptions are quite different in nature and it is good to understand why we need them. It can be argued that assumptions are important for two main reasons, which we can classify as theoretical and diagnostic reasons. In the first case, we need the set of ideal conditions to show certain theoretical results such as unbiasedness, consistency and asymptotic normality of estimators. However, in real life, assumptions might not hold true. A slight deviation could not be extremely problematic, but what if we are actually far off from the ideal conditions? This brings us to the second case, the diagnostic reason. During this course, you will learn how to check and test the assumptions. Moreover, you learn how to study the effects of violations on estimators and test statistics in a controlled environment. This way, you can judge the appropriateness of your model (and make adjustments, if needed). Let us consider the assumptions separately.

Assumption 1: The model is linear
It is important to note that the linearity is in terms of the parameters \(\beta\), not the variables \(X\). Interestingly, this means that nonlinear relationships between variables can be modelled using a linear regression model. Let’s consider a famous example in which there is a quadratic relationship between \(x\) and \(y\). Figure 1 displays this example.



Figure 1a shows the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\). Figure 1b shows the relationship between \(x^2\) and \(y\).


Figure 1a shows that linear regression between \(x\) and \(y\) is not meaningful. The blue line represents the estimated linear regression line, which is clearly not able to capture the relationship. However, if we instead run the regression \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x^{2}_{i} + u_{i},
\] we see that this relationship is close to linear. Consequently, the estimated linear regression line (in red) now shows an almost perfect fit. Of course, it is not always possible to recast in a nonlinear relationship into a linear regression model (where the variables are transformed). There are “linear models in disguise”, but sometimes there is need for a nonlinear regression model (not captured in this course). Because linearity is a so-called first-order approximation to the model, it often even forms the basis for nonlinear models (you will see some examples of such models [logit/probit/tobit] in Econometrics II). A main advantage of the linear regression model is its high degree of interpretability.


Assumption 2: The \(n \times k\) matrix \(X\) is nonrandom and has rank \(k\)
This assumption has two parts to it, which we will discuss separately. First, the matrix \(X\) is nonrandom. Note that this is a choice that we make for theoretical reasons, because our mathematical derivations are easier if we treat the independent variables as given. This is not something that you can check or test on data. We make this simplifying assumption to make our life easier (we circumvent conditioning, which we discuss in week 6 of the course) but it comes at the cost of a loss in generality.






NoteRelation between \(n\) and \(k\)





It is also implicit that the number of observations \(n\) is always larger than the number of regressors \(k\). If this was not the case, we would not be able to estimate the coefficients in the model. You can draw the analogy with solving a system of equations. If the pieces of information \(n\) are smaller than the number of unknowns \(k\), then the system cannot be solved. In case of equality \(n=k\), it is technically possible to find a solution but it is very undesirable in the estimation framework (some measures, such as the SER, could not even be computed) as there are no degrees of freedom left to test or validate the model’s accuracy.



Second, we assume that the \(n \times k\) matrix \(X\) has rank \(k\). The assumption dictates that all \(k\) columns are linearly independent. In other words, it is impossible to write a single column as a linear combination of all the other columns. Why is this important? Last week, we saw that the least-squares approximator is given by \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\). In the estimation framework, this formula remains the same as we will prove next week. Note that \(X'X\) is a \(k \times k\) matrix of full rank \(k\) (see Section A.3 in ITE for more details). We can only compute the inverse of \(X'X\) if it is nonsingular, i.e., if it has full rank.
In case we do have columns in \(X\) that are linear combinations of each other, we call it perfect multicollinearity. The wording is exactly saying what is going on: multiple columns are perfectly collinear.


Assumption 3: The \(n \times 1\) vector \(u\) has mean zero and variance \(\sigma^{2}I_{n}\)
The first part of the assumption, \(E(u) = 0\), is not really restrictive. Even if the errors had a non-zero population mean, its effect would be absorbed into the model’s intercept. Thus, it is convenient to assume without loss of generality. The second part of the assumption, \(\Var(u) = \sigma^{2}I_{n}\) tells us a couple of things. Note that the variance of a vector is a matrix with the separate variances on the diagonal, and the covariances on the off-diagonal elements. That is, \[
\Var(u) =
\begin{pmatrix}
\Var(u_{1}) & \Cov(u_{1},u_{2}) & \cdots & \Cov(u_{1}, u_{n}) \\
\Cov(u_{2}, u_{1}) & \Var(u_{2}) & \cdots & \Cov(u_{2}, u_{n}) \\
\vdots & \vdots &  & \vdots \\
\Cov(u_{n}, u_{1}) & \Cov(u_{n}, u_{2}) & \cdots & \Var(u_{n})
\end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma^{2} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \sigma^{2} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma^{2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Thus, we can see that \(\Cov(u_{i}, u_{j}) = 0\) for all \(i \neq j\). In words, this means that the error terms of respondents \(i\) and \(j\) are not correlated. Ideally, we also do not want a relation between two or more respondents. This can be motivated from both a theoretical and practical perspective. If the data is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), then this reflects that the respondents come from the same population (they have an identical distribution) but their responses are made independently of one another.
Another important feature is that \(\Var(u_{i}) = \sigma^{2}\) for all \(i = 1, \ldots, n\). This is a property called homoskedasticity. In empirical work, this assumption might fail and that is why we will revisit it towards the end of the course. For now, we assume that there is a constant variance for all the error terms.


Assumption 4: The \(n \times 1\) vector \(u\) follows a multivariate normal distribution
In the book, three main reasons are given for this assumption:

The normal distribution is easy to work with;
The normal distribution fits well in the context of measurement errors;
The normal distribution serves as a second-order approximation to an arbitrary density function (certainly in the center of the distribution).

During this course, we will benefit a lot from the normal distribution and its characteristics. In particular, Assumption 3 and 4 together imply that the disturbances \(u_{i}\) are not only uncorrelated, but in fact independent (a stronger property!). But we will use more properties, and one of the most important ones is that linear combinations of normal variables are again normally distributed. More information about the (multivariate) normal distribution is in Section B.3 of ITE. However, it is important to mention that normality is often seen as a “luxury assumption”. It simplifies a lot of derivations, but it is by no means necessary to show important results such as unbiasedness, consistency, and asymptotic normality of least-squares estimators. In various empirical applications (e.g., financial returns) the assumption of normally distributed error terms is not appropriate. For this reason, we will reconsider this assumption later on in the course.


Assumption 5: If we let \(Q_{n} = X'X/n\), then \(Q_{n} \to Q\) as \(n \to \infty\), where \(Q\) is a finite and positive definite \(k \times k\) matrix
We will only need this assumption when we discuss asymptotics. However, let us try to get some intuition of what is going on here. Consider the simple linear regression model in matrix form. This means \(X = (\imath : x)\) where \(\imath\) is an \(n \times 1\) vector of ones, and \(x\) an \(n \times 1\) vector containing \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\) (i.e., \(n\) observations on a single regressor). Since \(X\) is \(n \times 2\), we know that \(X'X\) is a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, which looks as follows: \[
X'X =
\begin{pmatrix}
\imath'\imath & \imath'x \\
x'\imath & x'x
\end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix}
n & \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} \\
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} & \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Let us have a look at the separate entries of this matrix. When \(n \to \infty\), we do not want any elements ‘to explode’ (i.e., diverge) but also not all shrink to zero (making the matrix singular and thus non-invertible). Note that \(\frac{1}{n}\) is exactly the right scaling to ensure that those two situations do not occur. That is, we obtain \[
Q_{n} = X'X/ n =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} \\
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} & \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}
\end{pmatrix},
\] where the element \((Q_{n})_{11} = 1\) is now constant (any other scaling would have caused diverging to \(\infty\) or convergence to zero), the element \((Q_{n})_{12} = (Q_{n})_{21} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\) is the sample mean which converges to the population mean \(E(x_{i})\) by the law of large numbers and the element \((Q_{n})_{22} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}\) does so similarly but then to \(E(x_{i}^{2})\). For now, this intuition suffices. We will discuss the assumption in more detail when we actually need it.

title: Week 2 - The linear regression model
text:
Model and data-generation process
It is important to understand the difference between a model and a data-generation process (DGP). As explained in the book, the DGP is the true process that generates the data. In reality, we almost never know the DGP (only in very simplified settings, or experimental setups). As econometricians, we use models to approximate the DGP and often we want to ask ourselves: “How well is my model performing for a certain DGP?”.
This means that, unlike real life, we will often assume that we know the DGP in this course. This way, we have the possibility to assess the performance of the model. Suppose that we are interested in measuring the effect of \(x\) on \(y\) as adequate as possible. If we suppose the DGP is given by \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i},
\tag{1}\] we could ask ourselves the question: “Suppose I misspecify my model by accidentally excluding the intercept, am I still able to recover the effect of \(x\) on \(y\) adequately?”. Thus, we know 1 is the truth, but we estimate instead \[
y_{i} = \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}.
\tag{2}\] Clearly, 2 is a restricted version of 1 by setting \(\beta_{1} = 0\). Thus, we would actually investigate whether such a restriction is appropriate in this case. How to do that, we will study later (from Section 2.14 onwards)!

title: Week 2 - The linear regression model
text:
Properties of estimators
As we mentioned before, approximation is very different from estimation. In the approximation context, data is nonrandom and thus it makes no sense to talk about concepts such as unbiasedness. However, if we assume that data are realizations of random variables, it means that every new draw results in a different data set. In other words, suppose two students are going to collect data at the VU, e.g., by asking \(n\) students to fill in a survey. The two students each manage to get a sample from the same population, but their samples are different because they asked different students to complete the survey. However, both samples are a valid realization of a random process. Thus, if we were to estimate a linear regression model by least squares on both samples, we want that estimator to perform well in both cases.
Unbiasedness intuitively means that our estimator equals the correct, true value on average. In technical terms, for a given parameter \(\theta\), we have \(E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\). To understand this, imagine that we could repeatedly draw new samples from the population and calculate \(\hat{\theta}\) for each sample. The average of these estimates would equal the true value \(\theta\). In other words, the estimator does not systematically overestimate or underestimate the value of the parameter.
This is an informal way to think about unbiasedness, but it is important to distinguish it from asymptotic concepts such as consistency: unbiasedness concerns the estimator’s average over repeated samples, whereas consistency concerns the behavior of the estimator as the number of observations of a single sample grows (and is evaluated at \(n \to \infty\)).

Unbiasedness of the least-squares estimator in the simple linear regression model
How can we prove that an estimator is unbiased? Let us characterize this for the least-squares estimator of the slope in the simple linear regression model. We assume that the model and the DGP coincide. The least-squares estimator of \(\beta_{2}\) is given by \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}.
\] Based on the DGP, \(y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}\) and \(\overline{y} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}\overline{x} + \overline{u}\) by taking the sample average. Plugging these expressions into the estimator, yields \[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\beta}_{2} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})[(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}) - (\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}\overline{x} + \overline{u})]}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
                &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})[(\beta_{2}(x_{i} - \overline{x}) + u_{i} - \overline{u})]}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
                &= \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(u_{i} - \overline{u})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
                &= \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}},
\end{aligned}
\] because \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})\overline{u} = \overline{u}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x}) = \overline{u} \cdot (n\overline{x} - n\overline{x}) = \overline{u} \cdot 0 = 0\). If we now take expectations, we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
E(\widehat{\beta}_{2}) &= E \left(\beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \right) \\
                   &= E(\beta_{2}) + E \left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \right) \\
                   &= \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})E(u_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
                   & = \beta_{2},
\end{aligned}
\] where we used that \(X\) is nonrandom (and thus can be taken outside of the expectation operator) by Assumption 2 and \(E(u_{i}) = 0\) by Assumption 3. Since \(E(\widehat{\beta}_{2}) = \beta_{2}\), we have shown that the least-squares estimator \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\) is unbiased for the slope coefficient \(\beta_{2}\). Note how the assumption that \(X\) is nonrandom simplified the derivation a lot.


How to continue?
We have just shown unbiasedness of the least-squares estimator in the simple linear regression model. It is important that you are able to show unbiasedness of estimators throughout this course. However, we are about to take a different approach in the book. That is, we forget about everything we learnt in the framework of approximation. We don’t know the derived formulas anymore. We are going to continue as follows. Assume we have the linear regression model in general form \(y = X\beta + u\) and Assumption 1-5 hold. Our goal is to derive the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE). This means that we are interested in linear estimators, which are unbiased and have the lowest variance possible. We can find the BLUE by solving a contrained minimization problem. We are going to minimize the variance of a linear estimator, subject to the estimator being unbiased. How this exactly works, is explained in the last sections of this week.






Tip📚 Read in ITE



Read Section 2.8 and 2.9.

Section 2.8 motivates unbiased estimation and highlights some strengths and flaws of the concept.
Section 2.9 focuses on best unbiased estimation of a linear combination of the \(\beta\)s.

Why a linear combination of the \(\beta\)s and not just \(\beta\) itself? \(\beta\) is a parameter vector, while \(w'\beta\) is a scalar. We will see that standard methods in calculus can be used for scalar objects. For objects such as vectors and matrices, this is no longer possible and we need to resort to other proving styles. For this, we need the result on the linear combination of the \(\beta\)s first!

title: Short introduction
text:
How does this course fit in the curriculum?
In econometrics and data science, we are often interested in supervised learning problems such as \[
y = f(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}) + u,
\tag{1}\] where \(f\) describes a relationship between the predictors \((x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k})\) and the outcome variable \(y\), while \(u\) captures random deviations from this relationship. The general problem posed in (1) is to learn the unknown function \(f\). However, estimating a completely unrestricted function \(f\) is often a very complicated task that may require a large amount of data. Moreover, the resulting relationship can be difficult to interpret.
Therefore, we take a more structured approach in this course. First, we assume that the relationship can be summarized by a finite number of unknown parameters, which we denote \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_k\). Second, we make the simplifying assumption that the systematic relationship is linear. That is, \(f(x_{1},\ldots, x_{k}) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \ldots + \beta_{k} x_{k}\). This leads to the linear regression model \[
y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \ldots + \beta_{k} x_{k} + u.
\tag{2}\] This course will evolve completely around the model in (2). How can we estimate its parameters? How can we test hypotheses on these parameters? What properties do our estimators and tests have when sample size is very small or large? Why are assumptions on the model needed, and what action should we take whenever an assumption does not hold true? These are some of the questions that we will be answering in this course.
Maybe you now have the following thought: did we not simplify the problem too much? and rightfully so. Restricting ourselves to a linear model feels quite strong, does it not? This is where the good news comes in. You will see that the linear regression model is an extremely powerful tool. The imposed linearity ensures a high degree of interpretability and is thus intuitive to work with. On top of that, it is often a difficult-to-beat benchmark for prediction problems. Why exactly? You will also learn more about this in the upcoming weeks!


Notation
Before we get started, we need to clarify notation. Econometrics is at the intersection of various fields, which inherently means that there will be clashes in notation compared to some of your previous courses. For example, in statistics courses random quantities are often denoted by capital letters and their realizations by lowercase letters. However, courses on algebra typically use lowercase letters for scalars and vectors, while matrices are denoted by uppercase letters. In this course, we remain closest to the linear algebra conventions.
Of course, we wish to be as concise as possible, but there will be instances where a trade-off in notation has to be made. Unfortunately, this will not be to everyone’s pleasing as we all have different preferences. Let me provide a simple example.






NotePresenting the linear regression model



In (2), I decided to include an intercept \(\beta_{0}\) in the model because that is probably how you have seen it before. However, since we have \(k\) predictors, we now have \(k+1\) coefficients. Consequently, the term \(k+1\) will show up in a lot of formulas (e.g., measures of fit, test statistics). Alternatively, we could have taken \(\beta_{1}\) to be the intercept by defining \(x_{1} = 1\), such that it is no longer a random variable. In that case we only have \(k\) coefficients, which makes most expressions look nicer. This is how it is done in the book Introduction to the Theory of Econometrics that we follow in this course. In what follows, we will call it ITE.


In conclusion, the main intention is to keep expressions and derivations understandable and not cluttered with unnecessary complicated notation. More explanation about this is also included in the ITE book. In case of any ambiguity, clarification will always be offered.
Anything unclear? Please ask it during the classes! We always try our utmost best to prevent it from happening, but typos can sometimes emerge unfortunately. It is very much appreciated if you inform us about those too!

Exercise 1
(2.18 in ME) Let \(y = X_{1}\beta_{1} + X_{2}\beta_{2} + u\). Let \(\widehat{\beta}_{1r}\) be the estimator of \(\beta_{1}\) by regressing \(y\) on \(X_{1}\) alone. Let \(\widehat{\beta}_{1u}\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_{2u}\) be the estimators of \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) when \(y\) is regressed on both \(X_{1}\) and \(X_{2}\). Show that \(\Var(\widehat{\beta}_{1r}) \leq \Var(\widehat{\beta}_{1u})\). What is the implication of this result? You may use the fact that \(\Cov(\widehat{\beta}_{2u}, \widehat{\beta}_{1r}) = 0\).






CautionSolution





The full solution can be found in the book Mastering Econometrics, Exercise 2.18.





Exercise 2
(2.19 in ME) Suppose that the DGP is given by \[
y = X_{1}\beta_{1} + X_{2}\beta_{2} + u, \qquad u \sim N(0, \sigma^{2}_{u}I_{n}),
\] which we will refer to as the unrestricted model. We denote the least-squares estimator of \(\beta_{1}\) in this model by \(\widehat{\beta}_{1u}\). We also consider the restricted model \[
y = X_{1}\beta_{1} + u_{1},
\] and we denote the least-squares estimator of \(\beta_{1}\) in this model as \(\widehat{\beta}_{1r}\). It can be shown that \[
\text{bias}(\widehat{\beta}_{1r}) = (X_{1}'X_{1})^{-1}X_{1}'X_{2}\beta_{2},
\] and \[
\Var(\widehat{\beta}_{1u}) - \Var(\widehat{\beta}_{1r}) = \sigma^{2}_{u}\Delta,
\] where \[
\Delta = (X_{1}'X_{1})^{-1}X_{1}'X_{2}(X_{2}'M_{1}X_{2})^{-1}X_{2}'X_{1}(X_{1}'X_{1})^{-1},
\] and \(M_{1} = I_{n} - X_{1}(X_{1}'X_{1})^{-1}X_{1}'\).

Under which conditions is the restricted estimator \(\widehat{\beta}_{1r}\) unbiased?
Show that \(\Delta\) is positive semidefinite.
Use the given expressions to comment on the statement: ‘In a regression, it is always best to include as many explanatory variables as possible. After all, they might have some explanatory power on the dependent variable.’







CautionSolution





The full solution can be found in the book Mastering Econometrics, Exercise 2.19.





Exercise 3
(3.8 in ME) Production \(Q\) is determined by a Cobb-Douglas production function, which we estimate in logarithmic form as \[
\log Q_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{k}\log K_i + \beta_{l}\log L_i + u_i.
\] This yields the following result: \[
\widehat{\log Q} = 1.37 + \underset{(0.257)}{0.632}\log K + \underset{(0.219)}{0.452} \log L,
\] where the standard errors are in parentheses. We further have \(R^2 = 0.98\) and \(\Cov(\widehat\beta_{k}, \widehat\beta_{l}) = 0.055\).

Test the hypothesis that the output elasticities with respect to capital \(K\) and labor \(L\) are the same.
Test the hypothesis that there are constant returns to scale.







CautionShort solution






We find \(t = 2.85\), which is the realization of a \(t(n-3)\) distribution. We do not know the value of \(n\). If \(n\leq6\) then we do not reject the null hypothesis at the \(5\%\) significance level, but if \(n>6\) we do.
We find \(t = 0.18\), which is too small to be significant at any sample size, and we can therefore not reject the hypothesis of constant returns to scale.






Exercise 4
(3.9 in ME) Consider the linear regression model \[
y = X\beta + u,
\] where \(X\) is an \(n \times k\) matrix and \(\beta = (\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{k})'\). Show that the \(F\)-statistic for a single restriction \(\beta_{j} = 0\) is equal to the square of the \(t\)-statistic to test \(\beta_{j} = 0\).






CautionSolution





The full solution can be found in the book Mastering Econometrics, Exercise 3.9.





Exercise 5
Show that the test statistic \[
\frac{w'\widehat{\beta} - r}{\sqrt{s^{2}w'(X'X)^{-1}w}} \sim t(n-k)
\] reduces to \[
\frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j}}{\sqrt{s^{2}v_{jj}}} \sim t(n-k)
\] for the restriction \(\beta_{j} = 0\). Note that \(V = (X'X)^{-1}\).






CautionSolution





The restriction \(\beta_{j} = 0\) can be represented in the form \(w'\beta = r\) by choosing \(w = e_{j}\), where \(e_{j}\) is the \(k \times 1\) basis vector where the \(j\)-th entry is one and all other entries are zero, and \(r = 0\). Thus, in the numerator, we obtain \(w'\widehat{\beta} = e_{j}'\widehat{\beta} = \widehat{\beta}_{j}\).
Regarding the denominator, we note that \(w'(X'X)^{-1}w\) can be written as \(e_{j}'Ve_{j}\) in this case. We have \[
Ve_{j} =
\begin{pmatrix}
v_{1j} \\
v_{2j} \\
\vdots \\
v_{kj}
\end{pmatrix}
\qquad \text{ and }
e_{j}'Ve_{j} = v_{jj}.
\]
This gives the desired result.





Exercise 6
(3.10, 3.11, 3.12 in ME) Consider the model \(y = X\beta + u\). We impose the restriction \(R\beta=r\), where \(R\) has full row rank. The least-squares (LS) estimator of \(\beta\) in the restricted model is obtained by minimizing \((y-X\beta)'(y-X\beta)\) under the restriction \(R\beta=r\).

Show that the restricted LS estimator is given by \[
\tilde\beta  = \hat\beta - (X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r),
\] where \(\hat\beta\) is the estimator in the unrestricted model.
Show that \[
\tilde{u}=\hat{u} + X(X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r),
\] where \(\hat{u}\) denotes the residual vector from the unrestricted model and \(\tilde{u}\) the residual vector from the restricted model.
The \(F\)-statistic for testing the hypothesis \(R\beta=r\) is given by \[
F = \frac{(R\hat\beta - r)'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r)/m}{\hat{u}'\hat{u}/(n-k)} \sim F(m,n-k),
\] where \(\hat{u}\) is the residual vector from the unrestricted regression. Show that \(F\) can also be written as \[
F = \frac{(\tilde{u}'\tilde{u} - \hat{u}'\hat{u})/m}{\hat{u}'\hat{u}/(n-k)},
\] where \(\tilde{u}\) denotes the residual vector from the restricted regression.







CautionSolution






The objective function is \(\phi(\beta)=(y-X\beta)'(y-X\beta)\) and the constraint is \(R\beta-r=0\). Since we are essentially differentiating a square, it is common practice to minimize \(\phi(\beta)/2\), but this is for aesthetic convenience only. The Lagrangian is then \[
\psi(\beta)=(y-X\beta)'(y-X\beta)/2 -l'(R\beta-r),
\] where \(l\) is a vector of Lagrangian multipliers. Taking the derivative with respect to \(\beta\) gives \[
\frac{\partial\psi(\beta)}{\partial\beta'} = -(y-X\beta)'X -l'R,
\] so that the first-order conditions are \[
X'(y-X\beta) + R'l=0,
\qquad
R\beta=r.
\] To solve these two equations in the two unknowns \(\beta\) and \(l\), we premultiply the first equation by \(R(X'X)^{-1}\), giving \[
R(X'X)^{-1}R'l = - R(X'X)^{-1}X'(y-X\beta) = - (R\hat\beta - r),
\] where \(\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y\) is the estimator in the unrestricted model. Since the matrix \(R(X'X)^{-1}R'\) is nonsingular, we can solve \(l\) as \[
l = - (R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r),
\] so that \[
X'(y-X\beta) + R'l
= X'y-X'X\beta - R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r) =0,
\] from which we solve the restricted estimator as \[
\tilde\beta  = \hat\beta - (X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r).
\] To show that the matrix \(V=R(X'X)^{-1}R'\) is nonsingular, we argue as follows. Let \(A=(X'X)^{-1/2}R'\). Then, \(V=A'A\) and \(r(V)=r(A'A)=r(A)=r(R')=m\), where we used the facts that \(R\) has full row rank and that \(r(A'A)=r(A)\) for any matrix \(A\); see also Exercise A.15 in Mastering Econometrics. This shows that \(V\) is an \(m \times m\) matrix of rank \(m\), hence nonsingular.
We find \[
\tilde{\beta}  = \hat\beta - (X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r).
\] Premultiplying this expression by \(X\) yields \[
X\tilde\beta  = X\hat\beta - X(X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r).
\] Since \(\hat{u}=y-X\hat\beta\) and \(\tilde{u}=y-X\tilde\beta\), we then find \[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{u}
&= y-X\tilde\beta \\
&= y-X\hat\beta + X(X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r) \\
&= \hat{u} + X(X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r).
\end{aligned}
\]
We know that \[
\tilde{u} = \hat{u} + X(X'X)^{-1}R'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r).
\] In fact, this relationship is a decomposition, because the two vectors on the right-hand side are orthogonal to each other, which follows from the fact that \(X'\hat{u}=0\). Then, letting \(V=R(X'X)^{-1}R'\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{u}'\tilde{u}
&= \hat{u}'\hat{u} + (R\hat\beta - r)'V^{-1}R(X'X)^{-1}X'X (X'X)^{-1}R'V^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r)\\
&=\hat{u}'\hat{u} + (R\hat\beta - r)'V^{-1}VV^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r)\\
&=\hat{u}'\hat{u} + (R\hat\beta - r)'V^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r).
\end{aligned}
\] It follows that \[
\frac{(R\hat\beta - r)'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\hat\beta - r)/m}{\hat{u}'\hat{u}/(n-k)}
=
\frac{(\tilde{u}'\tilde{u} - \hat{u}'\hat{u})/m}{\hat{u}'\hat{u}/(n-k)}.
\]






Exercise 7
(3.18 in ME) Consider a sample of size \(n=12\) from the linear regression model \(y = X\beta + u\), where \(X = (\imath : x_{2} : x_{3})\). We know that \(\bar{x}_2=\bar{x}_3=0\), \(\bar{y}=2.5\), and \[
\begin{aligned}
x_{2}'x_{2}^{} &= 300, \qquad & x_{2}'x_{3}^{} &= -205,   \qquad  & x_{3}'x_{3}^{} &= 182,\\
x_{2}'y &= 3,          \qquad & x_{3}'y &= -12,           \qquad  & y'y &= 470.
\end{aligned}
\]

Find the least-squares (LS) estimate of \(\beta\).
Calculate \(s^{2}\), \(R^2\), and \(\bar{R}^2\).
Comment on the values of \(R^2\) and \(\bar{R}^2\). Are they plausible?

(Similar exercises in ME: 3.1, 3.14, 3.19)






CautionSolution






The matrix \(X'X\) is given by \[
X'X =
\begin{pmatrix}
n & \imath'x_{2} & \imath'x_{3} \\
\imath'x_{2} & x_{2}'x_{2}^{} & x_{2}'x_{3}^{} \\
\imath'x_{3} & x_{3}'x_{2}^{} & x_{3}'x_{3}^{}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
12 & \phantom{-}0 & \phantom{-}0 \\
0 & \phantom{-}300 & -205 \\
0 & -205 & \phantom{-}182
\end{pmatrix}.
\] This matrix is block-diagonal, and we write \[
X'X =
\begin{pmatrix}
12 & 0' \\ 0 & Z
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Z=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phantom{-}300 & -205 \\
-205 & \phantom{-}182
\end{pmatrix}.
\] The determinant of \(Z\) is \(|Z|=300 \times 182 - (-205)^{2} = 12575\), which is nonzero, so that \(Z\) and hence \(X'X\) are nonsingular. Thus, \[
(X'X)^{-1} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1/12 & 0' \\ 0 & Z^{-1}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Z^{-1}=
\frac{1}{12575}
\begin{pmatrix}
182 & 205 \\
205 & 300
\end{pmatrix},
\] and \[
X'y =
\begin{pmatrix}
\imath'y \\ x_{2}'y \\ x_{3}'y
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} \phantom{-}30 \\ \phantom{-}3 \\ -12
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Consequently, we obtain the LS estimates \[
\hat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y =
\begin{pmatrix}
5/2 \\ -1914/12575 \\ -2985/12575
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Let \(A=I_n-\imath\imath'/n\). Since \[
\begin{aligned}
e'e  &= y'y - \hat{\beta}'X'y = 470 - 77.392 = 392.608, \\
y'Ay &= y'y -n\,\bar{y}^2 = 470 -12\times(2.5)^2 = 395,
\end{aligned}
\] we find \[
\begin{aligned}
s^2       &= e'e/(n-k)= 392.608 / 9 = 43.623, \\
R^2       &= 1- e'e/y'Ay =1 - 392.608 / 395 =0.006, \\
\bar{R}^2 &= 1-\frac{s^2}{y'Ay/(n-1)} = 1 - \frac{43.623}{395/11} = -0.215.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since we have a model with intercept, we know that \(R^2 \in [0,1]\), and this is indeed the case here. The fact that \(R^2\) is close to zero means that the fit is not good. We also know that \(\bar{R}^2\) is not restricted to the \([0,1]\) interval and, when the fit is not so good, it can become negative - as it does here.

title: Week 3 - Exercises
text:
(B.26 in ME) Let \(Q\) be a random variable with \[
E(Q) = (n-k)\sigma^{2}, \qquad \Var(Q) = 2(n-k)\sigma^{4},
\] where \(0 < k < n\). Now define an estimator \(\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{m} = Q/m\) of \(\sigma^{2}\).

Compute the mean and variance of \(\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n-k}\) and \(\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n}\).
Compute the mean squared error of \(\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n-k}\) and \(\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n}\).
Determine \(m\) such that the estimator \(\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}\) has the lowest mean squared error.







CautionSolution






The mean and variance of \(Q/m\) are \[
E(Q/m)= E(Q)/m = (n-k) \sigma^2/m
\] and \[
\Var(Q/m) = \Var(Q)/m^2 = 2(n-k)\sigma^4/m^2.
\] This implies \[
\begin{aligned}
&E(\hat\sigma_{n-k}^2)   =(n-k)\sigma^2/(n-k) =\sigma^2, \\
&E(\hat\sigma_{n}^2)     =(n-k)\sigma^2/n <\sigma^2, \\
&\Var(\hat\sigma_{n-k}^2) =2(n-k)\sigma^4/(n-k)^2 =2\sigma^4/(n-k), \\
&\Var(\hat\sigma_n^2)     =2(n-k)\sigma^4/n^2.
\end{aligned}
\] The first estimator is unbiased, while the second estimator is biased and underestimates \(\sigma^2\). But the first estimator has a larger variance than the second estimator, because \(2/(n-k) > 2(n-k)/n^2\).
The bias of \(Q/m\) as an estimator of \(\sigma^2\) is \[
\text{bias}(Q/m)= E(Q/m) - \sigma^2=(n-k-m)\sigma^2/m,
\] and the mean squared error is \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{MSE}(Q/m)&= \Var(Q/m) +\text{bias}^2(Q/m) \\
&= [2(n-k)+(n-k-m)^2]\sigma^4/m^2.
\end{aligned}
\] Based on the general formula for the mean squared error, we find \[
\text{MSE}(\hat\sigma_{n-k}^{2}) = 2\sigma^4/(n-k)
\] and \[
\text{MSE}(\hat\sigma_{n}^{2})   = (2(n-k)+k^2)\sigma^4/n^2,
\] from which we see that \[
\text{MSE}(\hat\sigma_{n-k}^{2})<\text{MSE}(\hat\sigma_{n}^{2})
\iff
k>4 \text{ and } n>\frac{k(k-2)}{k-4},
\] which may or may not be the case depending on the values of \(n\) and \(k\).
Since \[
\text{MSE}(\hat\sigma_{m}^{2}) = \frac{[2(n-k)+(n-k-m)^2]\sigma^4}{m^2},
\] we find the optimal value of \(m\) by minimizing \[
f(m)=\frac{2(n-k)+(n-k-m)^2}{m^2}.
\] Differentiating \(f\) gives \[
\begin{aligned}
f'(m)
&=\frac{-2(n-k-m)m^2 - 4(n-k)m - 2(n-k-m)^2 m}{m^4}\\
&=\frac{-2(n-k-m+2)(n-k)}{m^3},
\end{aligned}
\] and this is zero if and only if \(m=n-k+2\). Hence, \(\hat\sigma_{n-k+2}^2\), although biased, has a smaller mean squared error than the unbiased estimator \(\hat\sigma_{n-k}^2\).







(1.12, 1.13 and 1.14 in ME) Suppose we minimize \[
\phi(\beta) = (y - X\beta)'(y - X\beta) + \lambda \beta'\beta,
\] where scalar \(\lambda > 0\). This is called ridge regression.

Show that \(b_{\text{ridge}} = (X'X + \lambda I_{k})^{-1} X'y\) is the solution to the minimization problem.
What could be the motivation to use ridge regression? Hint: what problem can occur in least squares but not in ridge? Compare \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\) and \(b_{\text{ridge}} = (X'X + \lambda I_{k})^{-1} X'y\).
Show that the ridge solution attains a minimum.

title: Week 1 - Exercises
text:
What is the difference between the simple and multiple linear regression model?
What is the difference between the error \(u_{i}\) and the residual \(e_{i}\)?
Which of the following is/are correct?

\(y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}\)
\(y_{i} = b_{1} + b_{2}x_{i} + e_{i}\)
\(\widehat{y}_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + e_{i}\)
\(e_{i} = y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i}\)
\(\widehat{y}_{i}  = b_{1} + b_{2} \widehat{x}_{i}\)

How do \(R^{2}\) and the SER describe the fit of a regression? What are their units of measurement?







CautionSolution






The word simple highlights that there is only one variable in \(X\), whereas there are multiple variables contained in \(X\) for multiple linear regression.
The term \(u_{i}\) is the true, unobserved error. For the simple linear regression model, \(u_{i} = y_{i} - \beta_{1} - \beta_{2}x_{i}\) and thus it is a function of the unknown \(\beta\) coefficients. The residual “attempts to make the error term observable” by computing \(e_{i} = y_{i} - b_{1} - b_{2}x_{i}\) instead. Note that they are distinctly different!

is correct, simple linear regression model. (2) is correct, essentially splitting \(y_{i}\) in a part explained by the model and a part not explained by the model: \(y_{i} = \widehat{y}_{i} + e_{i}\). (3) is incorrect. (4) is correct for the same reason as (2). Lastly, (5) is incorrect (keep in mind, \(x\) should never have a hat!).

\(R^{2} = 1 - \frac{RSS}{SST} \in [0,1]\), where the value \(0\) means no variation in \(y\) is explained by the model, while the value \(1\) means that all variation in \(y\) is explained by the model. \(R^{2}\) is essentially unit-free, but because it lies strictly in the interval \([0,1]\) is can be interpreted as a percentage. We also have \(SER = \sqrt{\frac{e'e}{n-k}}\), where \(k\) is the number of columns in \(X\). It approximates the standard error of the error term. A low SER means that a lot of variation in \(y\) is captured by the model. A high SER, i.e. close to the standard deviation of \(y\), means that almost no variation in \(y\) is explained by the model. The unit of measurement is the same as the one of the dependent variable (the residual is the vertical distance, while the SER considers a squared version of the residuals but then takes the square root).







We have seen two methods of measuring closeness: least squares (LS) and least absolute deviations (LAD). Determine for which method the following statements are true. Indicate why it is not true for the other method.

The method is robust against outliers.
The method has a unique solution.
The method has a closed-form solution.
The method is non-differentiable.







CautionSolution






LAD. Note that LS puts more weight on outliers, because they enter the objective function in squared form.
LS. Note that LAD generally has multiple solutions (the objective function is not strictly convex like LS).
LS. We computed \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\) as the closed-form solution for LS, but for LAD such a “formula” cannot be computed.
LAD. The absolute value sign in the objective function makes LAD not differentiable anywhere, whereas the square of LS allows us to compute the unique minimum using standard algebraic results.

Least-squares approximation
In these exercises, the goal is to make you familiar with deriving the least-squares approximator using both unit-specific and matrix notation.

Exercise 3
Consider the intercept-only model \[
y_{i} = \beta + u_{i}, \qquad (i=1,\ldots, n),
\] where \(\beta\) is a scalar.

Show that the least-squares solution is given by \(b = \overline{y}\) by minimizing \(\phi(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_{i}^{2}\).
Write the model in the form \(y = X\beta + u\) using vector and matrix notation. What are the dimensions of \(y\), \(X\), \(\beta\) and \(u\)?
We derived that the least-squares solution is given by \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\) for the general model \(y = X\beta + u\). Show that this expression reduces to \(b = \overline{y}\) for the intercept-only model.
Suppose we pretend that we do not know the least-squares solution for the general model. Use matrix notation to derive the least-squares approximator for the intercept only model by minimizing \(\phi(\beta) = u'u\).
Show that the objective function \(\phi(\beta) = u'u\) attains a minimum at the found solution.







CautionSolution
