\phi(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \beta)^{2}.
\] The first derivative is given by \[
\frac{d \phi(\beta)}{d \beta}  = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \beta),
\] where we used the chain rule. Setting the first derivative equal to zero and rearranging terms yields: \[
\frac{d \phi(\beta)}{d \beta}  = 0 \implies \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i   =  n  \beta.
\] So, \(b = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i = \overline{y}\).
We can write \[
\begin{pmatrix}
y_{1} \\ \vdots \\ y_{n}
\end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\ \vdots \\ 1
\end{pmatrix}
\beta +
\begin{pmatrix}
u_{1} \\ \vdots \\ u_{n}
\end{pmatrix},
\] so \(y\) and \(u\) are \(n \times 1\) vector, \(X\) reduces to a \(n \times 1\) vector in this case and \(\beta\) is a scalar (as was given already).
\(X\) is a vector of ones, so we have \(X = \imath\). Filling this into the formula of \(b\) yields \[
b = (\imath'\imath)^{-1}\imath'y.
\] Notice that \(\imath'\imath = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 = n\) and \(\imath'y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i}\) such that we obtain \(b = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i} = \overline{y}\).
The objective function is now \[
\phi(\beta) = (y - \beta \imath)'(y - \beta \imath) = y'y - 2\beta \imath'y - n\beta^{2},
\] where we can use simple calculus rules as \(\beta\) is a scalar. Thus, \[
\frac{d \phi(\beta)}{d \beta} = -2\imath'y + 2n\beta.
\] Setting this equal to zero and solving for \(\beta\) yields \(b= \frac{1}{n}\imath'y = \overline{y}\).
To see if we attain a minimum, we have to take a second derivative \[
\frac{d^{2} \phi(\beta)}{d \beta^{2}} = 2n > 0,
\] which is strictly larger than zero. This means that the extreme point found at d. indeed constitutes a minimum.






Exercise 4
Consider the no-intercept model \[
y_{i} = \beta x_{i} + u_{i}, \qquad (i=1,\ldots, n),
\] where \(\beta\) is a scalar.

Show that the least-squares approximator is given by \(b_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}\) by minimizing \(\phi(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_{i}^{2}\).
Write the model in the form \(y = X\beta + u\) using vector and matrix notation.
We derived that the least-squares approximator is given by \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\) for the general model \(y = X\beta + u\). Show that this expression reduces to \(b = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}\) for the no-intercept model.
Suppose we pretend that we do not know the least-squares solution for the general model. Use matrix notation to derive the least-squares approximator for the intercept only model by minimizing \(\phi(\beta) = u'u\).
Show that the objective function \(\phi(\beta) = u'u\) attains a minimum at the found solution.







CautionHint





This exercise can be solved analogously to Exercise 1.





Exercise 5
Consider the simple linear regression model \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i}, \qquad (i=1, \ldots, n).
\] Show that the least-squares approximator of \(\beta_{2}\) can be written as \[
b_{2} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x} \ \overline{y}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2} - \overline{x}^{2}} = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_{x}^{2}},
\] where \(s_{xy}\) is the sample covariance of \(x\) and \(y\), and \(s^{2}_{x}\) is the sample variance of \(x\).






CautionHint





The following strategy could be useful:

Write down the formulas for \(s_{xy}\) and \(s_{x}^{2}\), such that you know what to work towards.
Start by showing \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x} \ \overline{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})\).
In an analogous way, you can show \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2} - \overline{x}^{2} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}\).
Combine the results and make sure you have the correct scaling.

Remark and hint: If you want to write \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x} \ \overline{y}\) as \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})\), you might want to make use of a technique called telescoping. That is, you may want to add and subtract the same term. In this case, the term would be \(\overline{x} \ \overline{y}\). Try to understand why it is useful to do this.





Exercise 6

For the simple linear regression model, show that the least-squares approximation yields \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\), where \(\overline{y}\) is the sample average of \(y\) and \(\overline{\widehat{y}}\) the average of the predicted values.
Show that this result extends to the general linear regression model with \(k\) regressors.







CautionSolution






Least-squares approximation leads to two first-order conditions: \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i} = 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}e_{i} = 0\). The first one is crucial to show this result. Note that we have \[
y_{i} = \underbrace{b_{1} + b_{2}x_{i}}_{:= \widehat{y}_{i}} + e_{i},
\] i.e. we can write \(y_{i}\) as its fitted/predicted value \(\widehat{y}_{i}\) (part explained by the model) plus the residual \(e_{i}\) (part not explained by the model). If we sum over all \(i=1,\ldots, n\) and multiply by \(\frac{1}{n}\), we obtain: \[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{y}_{i} + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i}.
\] The last term equals zero by the first-order condition, thus \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\).
Similarly, we have \(y = Xb + e\) for the general model with \(k\) regressors. This translates to \(y = \widehat{y} + e\). To obtain sample means, we can write \[
\frac{1}{n}\imath'y = \frac{1}{n}\imath'\widehat{y} + \frac{1}{n} \imath'e,
\] where \(\imath\) is a \(n \times 1\) vector of ones. We note that \(\imath'e = 0\) by the first-order conditions (i.e., the constant term is ortogonal to the residual vector \(e\). In fact, all regressors \(X\) are orthogonal to \(e\)). Thus, \(\frac{1}{n}\imath'y = \frac{1}{n}\imath'\widehat{y}\).

Show that \(MM = M\) by writing out the product.

title: What is econometrics?
text:
Before we get started and dig into all types of mathematics and statistics, it is good to get a feeling of what econometrics is all about and how it came into existence.

Definition
Econometrics is defined as the application of mathematics and statistical methods to the empirical analysis of economic data. Christ (1966) describes it as producing economic statements that either explain the behavior of variables we have already seen, or forecast behavior that we have not seen, or both. Alternatively, Chow (1983) calls it the art and science of using statistical methods for the measurement of economic relations.
Christ’s definition is nice in the sense that it focuses on two main aspects of econometrics: finding relationships between variables on the one hand, and prediction on the other hand. However, Chow’s phrasing points out another crucial aspect: measurement. It is a quantitative exercise to express these relationships and they always involve some sense of uncertainty. Moreover, models are defined by assumptions and it is important to realize what our goal is. For example, if we want to identify causal relationships between variables, strict conditions have to be met (causality is arguably one of the most difficult tasks in econometrics), while this is less so the case when we want to perform prediction.


Short history
Ragnar Frisch (1895 - 1973) coined the term econometrics in 1926 and established it as a subject in the sense in which it is known today. Together with Jan Tinbergen (1903 - 1994), he won the first Nobel Prize in Economics in 1969 for having developed and applied dynamic models for the analysis of economic processes.
In his honor, the Tinbergen institute was founded in 1987. It is the graduate school and research institute for Economics and Business operated jointly by the Schools of Economics and Econometrics of Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR), University of Amsterdam (UvA) and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (VU).


Purposes
Let us consider some examples how econometrics can be used.






TipExample 1: The consumption function





In macroeconomics, consumption \(C\) is often represented as a linear function output \(Y\): \(C = c_{0} + c_{1}Y\), where the \(c_{1}\) is the propensity to consume. For economists, it is important to know how the fraction of disposable income that househould are willing to spend on consumption remains fixed or changes over time.









TipExample 2: The Cobb-Douglas production function





In microeconomics, the production function is often represented as \(Y = A K^{\alpha}L^{\beta}\), where \(K\) denotes capital, \(L\) labour and \(A\) is total factor productivity. The \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are parameters that provide important information (output elasticities). More precisely, they determine the so-called returns to scale. If \(\alpha + \beta = 1\), there are constant returns to scale. If the sum falls below one, returns are decreasing; if the sum is greater than one, returns are increasing. It is good to know whether doubling the inputs indeed leads to at least twice the input, and econometrics can be used to estimate the parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).









TipExample 3: Investments and the interest rate





In economics, it is well-known that there is a negative relationship between investments (\(I\)) and the interest rate (\(r\)). The rationale behind is that if the interest rate is high, it costs a lot to borrow money and investments stay low. However, is the effect of a unit-increase in the interest rate on investments the same from \(1\%\) to \(2\%\) compared to \(6\%\) to \(7\%\)? If this is not the case, one may need a nonlinear model or include a nonlinear term in a linear model, e.g. \(I = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}r + \beta_{2} r^{2} + u\), where \(u\) is the error term (still to come!)









TipExample 4: The Central Bank





Central banks determine the interest rates and therefore they want to see how a change impacts the economic system. From economics, it is expected that interest (\(r\)) going up results in less investments (\(I\)). This in turn decreases capital (\(K\)) as no more new machines are acquired, which translates in overall economic output (\(Y\)) going down. Using historical data, econometricians can perform so-called impulse-response analyses to investigate how variables change over time for different changes in the interest rate. This way, one can analyze different scenarios of interest (pun intended).









TipExample 5: Forecasting prices





Should you buy a new house or car now or should you still wait? Using historical data, econometricians can make forecasts of prices. In the current era, econometric models and other data science methods (such as neural networks, support vector machines, etc.) are often competing to provide “the best” forecasts. Which methods performs best depends completely on the properties of the data.





How can we do this?
Suppose we are interested in a random variable \(y\) and hypothesize that a set of \(k\) variables \(X = (x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{k})\) provide information about \(Y\). Then we can relate \(X\) and \(y\) in the following way: \[
y = f(X) + u.
\] The choice of \(f(\cdot)\) determines the type of model, whereas \(u\) allows for possible deviations since the relation between \(X\) and \(y\) is probably not perfect.
In this course, we restrict our attention to the linear regression model \[
y = \underbrace{\beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \ldots + \beta_{k}x_{k}}_{:= f(X)} + u,
\] which is the main workhorse in economics. This is mostly for the following reasons:

interpretability is high, as complexity is low;

instead of estimating a function, we have to estimate a low number of parameters;
it is a solid benchmark that is difficult to beat.



Types of data
To run analyses, we collect realizations of our random variables, which we call data. We distinguish three main categories of data:

Cross sections: data on different units at a single time period. Example: GDP of several EU countries in 2026.
Time series: data for a single entity collected at multiple time periods. Example: GDP of the Netherlands from 1980 to 2026.
Panel: data for multiple entities in which each entity is observed at two or more time period. Example: GDP of several EU countries from 1980 to 2026.

In this course, we only consider cross-sectional data.

From statistics to econometrics
If you are a student in the BSc EOR or EDS, you followed year a course in statistics during the second semester. In a lot of cases, your goal was to infer information on a random variable, say \(X\). Using a sample \((X_{1},\ldots, X_{n})\), various characteristics of the underlying population distribution were unraveled. Let’s have a look at a simple example.






CautionExample

title: Welcome to Econometrics I!
text:
Preface
The course Econometrics I (E_EOR2_TR1) has been taught in a specific way for several years. During the first period, the simple linear regression model was discussed based on the book “Introduction to Econometrics” by James H. Stock and Mark W. Watson. The first chapters consider the basics of the regression model with only one independent variable, where the model is presented for a single cross-sectional unit. In the second period, the model got extended to include multiple regressors and similar topics were treated. However, the book “Introduction to the Theory of Econometrics” (ITE, henceforth) by Jan R. Magnus made use of vector and matrix notation to represent the model.
Whereas one could argue that it can be beneficial to see some topics repeated, the setup created a certain disconnection between the materials in both periods. This should ideally not be the case, as the notation should not play such a dominant role in understanding the linear regression model. On the contrary, the two different notations should be complementary and during the course we will see several examples for which it is more convenient to use one over the other. Generally, expressions are a bit more intuitive using unit-specific notation while formulas are more compact based on vector and matrix notation.
In the new setup, we study the linear regression model using both forms of notation simultaneously. We start with the multiple linear regression from the outset and treat the simple linear model as a specific case, because it enhances our general understanding. In the case of a single regressor, linear regression can be represented by a line and meaningful graphs can be computed. When there are more explanatory variables, it becomes much more difficult to express the model graphically.
We follow the Introduction to the Theory of Econometrics book by Jan R. Magnus and this website provides all supporting material based on unit-specific notation. Thus, “Introduction to Econometrics” by James H. Stock and Mark W. Watson is no longer considered a mandatory reading, but definitely stays in the list of recommended readings. It provides a nice and comprehensible introduction to the topic of linear regression. Hence, for those that need more explanations and examples, or for those that just want to know more, the book can provide exactly that.
I hope you enjoy the course! The main goal is to provide you with a solid basis in one of the main workhorses of econometrics: the linear regression model. If you plan to take more econometrics courses in the future, I can promise you that this model will come back very often. Sometimes it needs to be adapted to properties of the data (e.g. censored/truncated/categorical data) or the type of data (e.g. time series or panel data) that you have at your disposal, but most models (even nonlinear ones!) are rooted in the linear regression model. Good luck studying and have fun!
Amsterdam, May 21, 2026
Sean Telg

Should I still buy the book or is this website sufficient?
It is important that you still buy the book Introduction to the Theory of Econometrics, because it forms the basis of this course. This website provides supporting material and extra explanations. It can by no means be seen as a replacement of the book.


Do all exercises come with solutions?
The majority of the exercises have solutions. The remaining exercises come with short solutions or hints. We will discuss them together in class. Full solutions will not be posted on this website or on Canvas.

title: Week 2 - Exercises
text:
Let \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\), and let \(e = y - Xb\) be the vector of residuals and \(\hat{y} = Xb\) the vector of predictors. Show that:

\(\widehat{y}\) and \(e\) are orthogonal to each other.
\(\widehat{y} = Py\) and \(e = My\), where \(P\) and \(M\) are symmetric idempotent matrices satisfying \(MP = 0\).
\(y'y = \widehat{y}'\widehat{y} + e'e\).
\(Ae = e\) if and only if the regression contains a constant term; more precisely, if \(\imath\) is a linear combination of the columns of \(X\).
\(y'Ay = \hat{y}'A\hat{y} + e'e\), if the regression contains a constant term, which we usually write as \(\text{SST} = \text{SSE} + \text{SSR}\).







CautionShort solution






\(\widehat{y} = Xb\), so \(\widehat{y}'e = b'X'e\), now \(X'e = 0\) by first order conditions of least squares. One can see this explicitly by substituting \(y - Xb\) for \(e\) and writing it out.
\(\widehat{y} = Xb = X(X'X)^{-1}X'y\), so \(P = X(X'X)^{-1}X'\) and thus \(M = I_{n} - P\). It is easily verifiable that \(P\) is, just like \(M\), symmetric and idempotent (which we already showed in class). Note that \(MP = (I_{n} - P)P = P - PP = P - P = 0\), as \(P\) is idempotent.
Write \(y = \widehat{y} + e\) and note that it is a decomposition (that is what you showed in the first subquestion).
Note that \(Ae = e\) if and only if \(\imath'e = \imath'My = 0\), which occurs if and only if \(M\imath = 0\).

If \(\imath\) is a linear combination of columns in \(X\), then \(\imath = Xc\) for some \(c\) and indeed \(MXc = 0\) as \(MX=0\).
Conversely, if \(M\imath = 0\), then writing out this equation yields \(\imath = X(X'X)^{-1}X'\imath\), which is a linear combination of the columns of \(X\).

Since \(Ae = e\) and \(\hat{y}'e = 0\) (orthogonality), one immediately gets the desired result in the same way as in c.

Empirical applications

Exercise 2
Suppose that a researcher, using data on class size (CS) and average test scores from 50 third-grade classes, obtains the following least squares output: \[
\widehat{Testscore} = 640.3 - 4.93 \times CS.
\]

A classroom has \(25\) students. What is the prediction for that classroom’s average test score?
Last year a classroom had \(21\) students, and this year it has \(24\) students. What is the regression’s prediction for the change in the classroom’s average test score? Is this prediction reliable? Motivate your answer.
The sample average of the class sizes across the 50 classrooms is \(22.8\). What is the sample average of the test scores across the \(50\) classrooms? Hint: Use the least-squares approximator of \(\beta_{1}\).







CautionSolution






\(\widehat{Testscore} = 640.3 - 4.93 \times 25 = 517.05\).
Similarly as in a., we can compute: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\widehat{Testscore} = 640.3 - 4.93 \times 21 = 536.77, \\
&\widehat{Testscore} = 640.3 - 4.93 \times 24 = 521.98,
\end{aligned}
\] which are the predicted test scores for \(CS = 21\) and \(CS = 24\), respectively. The predicted change is then \(521.98 - 536.77 = -14.79\). Note that this predicted change of \(-14.79\) in test score is not reliable. If the number of students is the only aspect that changes, we want to know the effect of increasing class size from \(21\) to \(24\), while keeping all other relevant factors fixed. This is the ceteris paribus interpretation. Ideally, we would therefore use a model such as \[
TestScore = \beta_1 + \beta_2 CS + \beta_3 QualityOfTeacher + \beta_4 QualityOfMaterial + \cdots + u^{*}.
\] In this model, \(\beta_2\) measures the expected change in test score associated with a one-student increase in class size, holding the other factors fixed. Therefore, increasing class size from \(21\) to \(24\) students corresponds to an estimated change of \(3\hat{\beta}_2\). In the simple regression \[
TestScore = \beta_1 + \beta_2 CS + u,
\] the error term \(u\) contains factors such as teacher quality and material quality. If these factors are correlated with class size, then \(u\) is correlated with \(CS\). For example, if larger classes tend to have worse teachers and worse materials, the negative relationship between class size and test scores partly reflects these other factors. The simple regression therefore cannot isolate the ceteris paribus effect of class size. Thus, the estimate \(-14.79 = 3\hat{\beta}_2\) from the simple regression should not be interpreted as the expected change in test score when an otherwise identical classroom goes from \(21\) to \(24\) students. It reflects the observed relationship between class size and test scores, which may also capture systematic differences in teacher quality, materials, and other factors between classrooms.
Note that \[
\hat{\beta}_{1} = \overline{y} - \hat{\beta}_{2}\overline{x},
\] which can be rewritten to \[
\begin{aligned}
\overline{y} &= \hat{\beta}_{1} + \hat{\beta}_{2}\overline{x} \\
          &= 640.3 - 4.93 \times 22.8 = 527.90.
\end{aligned}
\]






Exercise 3
A regression of average weekly earnings (\(AWE\), measured in dollars) on age (measured in years) using a random sample of college-educated full-time workers aged \(25-65\) yields the following output: \[
\widehat{AWE} = 696.7 + 9.6 \times Age.
\]

\(936.7\) and \(1128.7\), respectively.

Note that both \(SSE\) and \(SST\) are measured in \(dollar^{2}\), i.e. the squared unit of the dependent variable \(Y\). The unit of measurement of the \(SER\) is dollars; it has the same unit of measurement as the dependent variable \(Y\).
The errors likely have a right-skewed distribution, because there are some persons with relatively high earnings, whereas no persons have negative earnings (assuming no self-employed persons with large losses). The kurtosis (fatness of the tail) is also expected to be larger than under the normal distribution due to this.






Exercise 4
In a course on microeconomics, you have seen the Cobb-Douglas production function \[
Q = \alpha K^{\beta_{1}}L^{\beta_{2}},
\] where \(Q\) denotes output, \(K\) is capital, and \(L\) is labor. We wish to estimate \(\alpha\), \(\beta_{1}\), and \(\beta_{2}\) based on \(n\) observations on \((Q_{i}, K_{i}, L_{i})\). How can this be done?

Exercise 5

y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{1}^{2} + u,

An advantage of the multiple linear regression model is that it facilitates ceteris paribus analysis. Why is this difficult here?

Determine how a change in \(x_{1}\) affects \(y\). At which value of \(x_{1}\) does the function take its maximum?
Given an example of an empirical application where this modeling technique might be appropriate.

text: Residuals

title: Week 2 - Exercises
text:
Exercise 6
Consider the standard linear regression model \(y = X\beta + u\), where \(y\) and \(u\) are of order \(n \times 1\), \(\beta\) is of order \(k \times 1\), and \(X\) is an \(n \times k\) matrix with full column rank. We assume that \(E(u) = 0\) and \(\Var(u) = \sigma^{2} I_{n}\).

Show that the least-squares residuals \(e\) are equal to \(My\) and \(Mu\).
Compute the mean and variance of the residuals \(e\).
Show that the variance matrix of \(e\) cannot have full rank and explain why.







CautionSolution






The residuals are defined as \(e = y - X\hat{\beta}\) with \(\hat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\). Therefore, \[
\begin{aligned}
e &= y - X(X'X)^{-1}X'y = (I_{n} - X(X'X)^{-1}X')y \\
  &= My = M(X\beta + u) = Mu,
\end{aligned}
\] since \(MX = (I_{n} - X(X'X)^{-1}X')X = X - X = 0\). This also implies that \(X'e = X'Mu = 0\).
The mean of \(e\) is given by \[   
E(e)= E(Mu) = ME(u)=0,
\] and the variance of \(e\) can be computed as \[
\Var(e) = \Var(Mu) = M \Var(u) M = \sigma^2 M,
\] where we used the fact that \(M\) is symmetric and idempotent.
There are \(k\) linearly independent restrictions on the residuals, namely \(X'e = 0\), as shown in a. Given these constraints, the variance of \(e\) cannot have full rank. In fact, the rank is reduced by the number of linearly independent restrictions, as we can also see from \[
r(\Var(e))= r(\sigma^2 M) = r(M) = \text{tr}(M) = n-k,
\] as we have shown before. We like to think of \(e\) as a predictor of \(u\), but this is only partly successful, because \(\Var(u)\) is nonsingular, while \(\Var(e)\) is singular, since \(k\) degrees of freedom are lost when we estimate \(\beta\).

title: Week 2 - Exercises
text:
Best unbiased estimation

Exercise 9
Let \(\widehat{\theta}_{1}\) and \(\widehat{\theta}_{2}\) be two uncorrelated unbiased estimators of a parameter \(\theta\) with variances \(\sigma_{1}^{2}\) and \(\sigma_{2}^{2}\), respectively. What linear combination \[
\widehat{\theta} = w_{1} \widehat{\theta}_{1} + w_{2} \widehat{\theta}_{2}
\] is the best unbiased estimator of \(\theta\)?






CautionSolution





Since \(\widehat{\theta}_{1}\) and \(\widehat{\theta}_{2}\) are unbiased estimators of \(\theta\), we have \[
\begin{aligned}
E(\widehat{\theta}) &= w_{1} E(\widehat{\theta}_{1}) + w_{2} E(\widehat{\theta}_{2}) \\
&= w_{1}\theta + w_{2}\theta \\
&= (w_{1} + w_{2})\theta,
\end{aligned}
\] and since they are uncorrelated, we have \[
\begin{aligned}
\Var(\widehat{\theta})
&= w_{1}^{2}\Var(\widehat{\theta}_{1}) + w_{2}^2 \Var(\widehat{\theta}_{2}) \\
&= w_{1}^{2}\sigma_{1}^2 + w_2^{2}\sigma_{2}^2.
\end{aligned}
\] As \(\widehat{\theta}\) must be unbiased, we have \(w_1 + w_2=1\). Thus, we need to minimize \[
\phi(w_1)=w_{1}^{2}\sigma_{1}^2 + (1-w_1)^{2}\sigma_{2}^2.
\] Differentiating with respect to \(w_1\) gives \[
\phi'(w_1)=2w_{1}\sigma_{1}^2 - 2(1-w_{1})\sigma_{2}^2.
\] Setting the derivative to zero and solving gives \[
w_{1}^{*} = \frac{\sigma_{2}^2}{\sigma_{1}^2 + \sigma_{2}^2}.
\] This is indeed a minimum, because \(\phi''(w_1) = 2(\sigma_{1}^2 + \sigma_{2}^2) > 0\). Hence, the linear combination \[
\widehat{\theta} = \frac{\sigma_{2}^2}{\sigma_{1}^2 + \sigma_{2}^2}\widehat{\theta}_{1} + \frac{\sigma_{1}^2}{\sigma_{1}^2 + \sigma_{2}^2}\widehat{\theta}_{2}
\] is the minimum variance unbiased estimator of \(\theta\). For example, if \(\sigma_{1}^2 = 1\) and \(\sigma_{2}^2 = 3\), then \(w_{1} = 3/4\) and \(w_{2} = 1/4\), and the variance of \(\widehat{\theta}\) is \((3/4)^{2} \times 1 + (1/4)^{2} \times 3 = 3/4\), which is smaller than the variances of \(\widehat\theta_1\) and \(\widehat\theta_2\).

title: Week 4 - Exercises
text:
This week we start with some relatively short exercises on material covering the first three weeks. Because we are halfway the first part of the course, it is a good moment to check whether you can comfortably answer questions about this material.


For the simple linear regression model, show that \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x}\overline{y}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2} - \overline{x}^{2}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}.
\]






CautionShort solution





This solution only shows the numerator, the denominator is done analogously.
Note that \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x}\overline{y} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x}\overline{y} - \overline{x}\overline{y} + \overline{x}\overline{y} \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\overline{y} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i} \overline{x} + \overline{x}\overline{y} \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i}y_{i} - x_{i}\overline{y} - y_{i}\overline{x} - \overline{x}\overline{y}) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i}(y_{i} - \overline{y}) - \overline{x}(y_{i} - \overline{y})) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})
\end{aligned}
\] In the first equality, we make use of telescoping. In the second and third equality, we ensure that the first two terms are both expressed in terms of \(x_{i}\) and the last two terms in terms of \(\overline{x}\). This is convenient for collecting terms, which we do in the last two equalities.






In the linear regression model with intercept, show that \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\).






CautionSolution





Note that \(y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i} = e_{i}\). Taking sums and multiplying by \(\frac{1}{n}\) on both sides yields \[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{y}_{i} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i}.
\] We note that \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i} = 0\) by the first-order condition of least squares. Thus, \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\).
Alternatively, using vection notation, we can write \(y = \widehat{y} + e\). To obtain sums, we pre-multiply by \(\imath'\) to obtain \[
\imath'y = \imath'\widehat{y} + \imath'e.
\] Since \(\imath'e = 0\) by the first-order condition of least squares, we obtain \(\frac{1}{n}\imath'y = \frac{1}{n}\imath'\widehat{y}\).






In this exercise, we are going to investigate in more detail under what conditions \(SST = SSR + SSE\) holds.

Show that \[
SST = SSR + SSE + 2\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i})(\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y}).
\] Hint: Use telescoping.
Evaluate for the following three models whether the equation reduces to \(SST = SSR + SSE\).


The simple linear regression model.
The intercept-only model.
The no-intercept model (with only one regressor).


Show that we can obtain the decomposition \(y'y = \widehat{y}'\widehat{y} + e'e\) without assuming a constant term, whereas \(SST = SSE + SSR\) can only derived when we do assume a constant term.







CautionHint






Write \(y_{i} - \overline{y}\) as \(y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i} + \widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y}\). Continue with writing out the quadratic term. This should yield the desired result.
Do we obtain \(SST = SSR + SSE\) for the three models?


Yes, because we have both first-order conditions.
Yes, one of the first-order conditions suffices.
No, generally not. One first-order condition is not enough.


Both results are in Section 1.8 of ITE. Note that least squares always gives \(\widehat{y}'e = 0\) (because \(X'e = 0\)), which is needed for the first decomposition. For the second one we need \(\imath'e = 0\) explicitly.







There is something interesting about the way that we define SSE, the explained sum of squares. In textbooks, you will often read \[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2}.
\] However, this definition is different from typical measures of variation. For example, TSS is defined as the sum of squared deviation from its own mean, i.e. \[
SST = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \overline{y})^{2}.
\] Let us study \(SSE\) a bit deeper.

Show that, in case of a constant term, \[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} = \widehat{y}'A\widehat{y}.
\]
What changes in a. whenever there is no constant term in the model?
In light of what we found out in this exercise, reconsider exercise 3b for the no-intercept model. Do you think the textbook measure of \(SSE\) is informative in this case?







CautionSolution






We can write \[
\widehat{y}'A\widehat{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{\widehat{y}})^{2},
\] by definition. However, with constant term, it is important to see that \(\imath'\widehat{y} = \imath'(y - e) = \imath'y - \imath'e = \imath'y\) because \(\imath'e = 0\) by the first-order condition of least squares.
As shown in a. and in exercise 2 of this week, we no longer have \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\) in case there is no constant term in the model.
Typically, measures of variation consider the variation around their own mean. In case of a constant term in the model, the definition \[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2},
\] is perfectly accurate because \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\) due to the first-order condition \(\imath'e = 0\). However, whenever there is no constant term, one could argue that \[
SSE^{*} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{\widehat{y}})^{2},
\] is a much more sensible measure of variation around the fitted values. In light of exercise 3b, this means the following. We used telescoping to show \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i} + \widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i})^{2} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} \\
&\quad \ +2\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i})(\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y}),
\end{aligned}
\] which we denoted as \(SSR + SSE + \text{additional term}\). However, note that for the no-intercept model, the definition \(SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2}\) is arguably not appropriate. Thus, the decomposition does not only fail in terms of the additional term that does not disappear, but the measure of \(SSE\) could be considered questionable/inappropriate as a measure of explained variation.







Show that the OLS estimator for \(\beta_{2}\) in the simple linear regression model can also be written as \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \overline{y})x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}
\] Hint: You may start from \(\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}\).






CautionHint





The solution follows directly from writing out the numerator.






Suppose you demean the independent and dependent variable. Then you estimate a no-intercept model on this data, which we denote (\(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}\)). Show that the estimated slope coefficient for this model is the same as the estimated slope in a simple linear regression model on the original data (not demeaned).






CautionSolution





If we estimate a no-intercept model, the estimator for the slope coefficient is given by \[
\widehat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde{x}_{i}\tilde{y_{i}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde{x}_{i}^{2}}.
\] Since the variables are demeaned, we have \(\tilde{x}_{i} = x_{i} - \overline{x}\) and \(\tilde{y}_{i} = y_{i} - \overline{y}\). Plugging these expressions in the formula for \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\) yields the (by now, well-known) estimator \[
\widehat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}.
\]






Student A estimates the simple linear regression model \[
y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_i + u_i, \qquad (i=1,\ldots,n),
\] by least squares and finds the estimators \(\widehat{\beta}_{1}\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\). Student B instead estimates the linear regression model \[
y_i = \delta_1 + \delta_2 z_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad (i=1,\ldots,n),
\] by least squares, where \(z_{i} = c x_{i}\) for \(c > 0\), i.e. \(z_{i}\) is a rescaled version of \(x_{i}\). She denotes the estimators \(\widehat{\delta}_{1}\) and \(\widehat{\delta}_{2}\).

Show that \(\widehat{\delta}_{2} = c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2}\) and \(\widehat{\delta}_{1} = \widehat{\beta}_{1}\).
How would the results change when \(c < 0\)?
How do the \(SER\) and \(R^2\) of both models relate?







CautionSolution






Note that \[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\delta}_{2} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (z_{i} - \overline{z})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (z_{i} - \overline{z})^{2}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c x_{i} - c \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c x_{i} - c \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c(x_{i} - \overline{x}))(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c(x_{i} - \overline{x}))^{2}} = \frac{1}{c} \times \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2}. \\
\widehat{\delta}_{1} &= \overline{y} - \widehat{\delta}_{2}\overline{z} = \overline{y} - c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2} \times c \overline{x} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta}_{2}\overline{x} = \widehat{\beta}_{1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
From the results in a., we can see that a negative value of \(c\) results in a new slope that has opposite slope. The intercept is not affected.
The SER could only be different if both models generate different fitted values. However, note that \[
\widehat{y}_{i}^{(2)} = \widehat{\delta}_{1} + \widehat{\delta}_{2}z_{i} = \widehat{\beta}_{1} + c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2} \times c x_{i} = \widehat{\beta}_{1} + \widehat{\beta}_{2}x_{i} = \widehat{y}_{i}^{(1)}.
\] If the models generate the same fitted values, they also generate the same residuals. Thus since the SSR and SST is the same for both models, their \(R^{2}\) values should also be the same.







During the course, we often consider the situation of correct specification, i.e. the data-generation process and the model coincide. Let us consider a situation in which this is not true. Suppose the data-generation process is given by \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i},
\] whereas the model that we estimate is the no-intercept model \[
y_{i} = \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i}.
\] Is the least-squares estimator of \(\beta_{2}\) in our model unbiased for the true value of \(\beta_{2}\) in the data-generation process?






CautionSolution





The estimator of the slope coefficient based on the no-intercept model is given by \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}.
\] However, the data is generated according to \(y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i}\). Plugging this into the estimator yields \[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\beta}_{2} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} \\
                    &= \beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} + \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\] We proceed to take expectations: \[
\begin{aligned}
E(\widehat{\beta}_{2}) &= E \left(\beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} + \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} \right) \\
&= \beta_{2} + \beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}E(u_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} \\
&= \beta_{2} + \beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}},
\end{aligned}
\] where we used that \(x_{i}\) is nonrandom by Assumption 2.2 and \(E(u_{i}) = 0\) by Assumption 2.3. Thus, \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\) is biased and the bias equals \(\beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}\)

title: Week 4 - Exercises
text:
This week we start with some relatively short exercises on material covering the first three weeks. Because we are halfway the first part of the course, it is a good moment to check whether you can comfortably answer questions about this material.


For the simple linear regression model, show that \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x}\overline{y}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2} - \overline{x}^{2}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}.
\]






CautionShort solution





This solution only shows the numerator, the denominator is done analogously.
Note that \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x}\overline{y} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x}\overline{y} - \overline{x}\overline{y} + \overline{x}\overline{y} \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\overline{y} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i} \overline{x} + \overline{x}\overline{y} \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i}y_{i} - x_{i}\overline{y} - y_{i}\overline{x} - \overline{x}\overline{y}) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i}(y_{i} - \overline{y}) - \overline{x}(y_{i} - \overline{y})) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})
\end{aligned}
\] In the first equality, we make use of telescoping. In the second and third equality, we ensure that the first two terms are both expressed in terms of \(x_{i}\) and the last two terms in terms of \(\overline{x}\). This is convenient for collecting terms, which we do in the last two equalities.






In the linear regression model with intercept, show that \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\).






CautionSolution





Note that \(y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i} = e_{i}\). Taking sums and multiplying by \(\frac{1}{n}\) on both sides yields \[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat{y}_{i} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i}.
\] We note that \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i} = 0\) by the first-order condition of least squares. Thus, \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\).
Alternatively, using vection notation, we can write \(y = \widehat{y} + e\). To obtain sums, we pre-multiply by \(\imath'\) to obtain \[
\imath'y = \imath'\widehat{y} + \imath'e.
\] Since \(\imath'e = 0\) by the first-order condition of least squares, we obtain \(\frac{1}{n}\imath'y = \frac{1}{n}\imath'\widehat{y}\).






In this exercise, we are going to investigate in more detail under what conditions \(SST = SSR + SSE\) holds.

Show that \[
SST = SSR + SSE + 2\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i})(\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y}).
\] Hint: Use telescoping.
Evaluate for the following three models whether the equation reduces to \(SST = SSR + SSE\).


The simple linear regression model.
The intercept-only model.
The no-intercept model (with only one regressor).


Show that we can obtain the decomposition \(y'y = \widehat{y}'\widehat{y} + e'e\) without assuming a constant term, whereas \(SST = SSE + SSR\) can only derived when we do assume a constant term.







CautionHint






Write \(y_{i} - \overline{y}\) as \(y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i} + \widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y}\). Continue with writing out the quadratic term. This should yield the desired result.
Do we obtain \(SST = SSR + SSE\) for the three models?


Yes, because we have both first-order conditions.
Yes, one of the first-order conditions suffices.
No, generally not. One first-order condition is not enough.


Both results are in Section 1.8 of ITE. Note that least squares always gives \(\widehat{y}'e = 0\) (because \(X'e = 0\)), which is needed for the first decomposition. For the second one we need \(\imath'e = 0\) explicitly.







There is something interesting about the way that we define SSE, the explained sum of squares. In textbooks, you will often read \[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2}.
\] However, this definition is different from typical measures of variation. For example, TSS is defined as the sum of squared deviation from its own mean, i.e. \[
SST = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \overline{y})^{2}.
\] Let us study \(SSE\) a bit deeper.

Show that, in case of a constant term, \[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} = \widehat{y}'A\widehat{y}.
\]
What changes in a. whenever there is no constant term in the model?
In light of what we found out in this exercise, reconsider exercise 3b for the no-intercept model. Do you think the textbook measure of \(SSE\) is informative in this case?







CautionSolution






We can write \[
\widehat{y}'A\widehat{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{\widehat{y}})^{2},
\] by definition. However, with constant term, it is important to see that \(\imath'\widehat{y} = \imath'(y - e) = \imath'y - \imath'e = \imath'y\) because \(\imath'e = 0\) by the first-order condition of least squares.
As shown in a. and in exercise 2 of this week, we no longer have \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\) in case there is no constant term in the model.
Typically, measures of variation consider the variation around their own mean. In case of a constant term in the model, the definition \[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2},
\] is perfectly accurate because \(\overline{y} = \overline{\widehat{y}}\) due to the first-order condition \(\imath'e = 0\). However, whenever there is no constant term, one could argue that \[
SSE^{*} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{\widehat{y}})^{2},
\] is a much more sensible measure of variation around the fitted values. In light of exercise 3b, this means the following. We used telescoping to show \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i} + \widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i})^{2} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} \\
&\quad \ +2\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{i})(\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y}),
\end{aligned}
\] which we denoted as \(SSR + SSE + \text{additional term}\). However, note that for the no-intercept model, the definition \(SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\widehat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2}\) is arguably not appropriate. Thus, the decomposition does not only fail in terms of the additional term that does not disappear, but the measure of \(SSE\) could be considered questionable/inappropriate as a measure of explained variation.







Show that the OLS estimator for \(\beta_{2}\) in the simple linear regression model can also be written as \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \overline{y})x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}
\] Hint: You may start from \(\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}\).






CautionHint





The solution follows directly from writing out the numerator.






Suppose you demean the independent and dependent variable. Then you estimate a no-intercept model on this data, which we denote (\(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}\)). Show that the estimated slope coefficient for this model is the same as the estimated slope in a simple linear regression model on the original data (not demeaned).






CautionSolution





If we estimate a no-intercept model, the estimator for the slope coefficient is given by \[
\widehat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde{x}_{i}\tilde{y_{i}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde{x}_{i}^{2}}.
\] Since the variables are demeaned, we have \(\tilde{x}_{i} = x_{i} - \overline{x}\) and \(\tilde{y}_{i} = y_{i} - \overline{y}\). Plugging these expressions in the formula for \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\) yields the (by now, well-known) estimator \[
\widehat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}.
\]






Student A estimates the simple linear regression model \[
y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_i + u_i, \qquad (i=1,\ldots,n),
\] by least squares and finds the estimators \(\widehat{\beta}_{1}\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\). Student B instead estimates the linear regression model \[
y_i = \delta_1 + \delta_2 z_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad (i=1,\ldots,n),
\] by least squares, where \(z_{i} = c x_{i}\) for \(c > 0\), i.e. \(z_{i}\) is a rescaled version of \(x_{i}\). She denotes the estimators \(\widehat{\delta}_{1}\) and \(\widehat{\delta}_{2}\).

Show that \(\widehat{\delta}_{2} = c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2}\) and \(\widehat{\delta}_{1} = \widehat{\beta}_{1}\).
How would the results change when \(c < 0\)?
How do the \(SER\) and \(R^2\) of both models relate?







CautionSolution






Note that \[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\delta}_{2} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (z_{i} - \overline{z})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (z_{i} - \overline{z})^{2}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c x_{i} - c \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c x_{i} - c \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c(x_{i} - \overline{x}))(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (c(x_{i} - \overline{x}))^{2}} = \frac{1}{c} \times \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} \\
&= c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2}. \\
\widehat{\delta}_{1} &= \overline{y} - \widehat{\delta}_{2}\overline{z} = \overline{y} - c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2} \times c \overline{x} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta}_{2}\overline{x} = \widehat{\beta}_{1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
From the results in a., we can see that a negative value of \(c\) results in a new slope that has opposite slope. The intercept is not affected.
The SER could only be different if both models generate different fitted values. However, note that \[
\widehat{y}_{i}^{(2)} = \widehat{\delta}_{1} + \widehat{\delta}_{2}z_{i} = \widehat{\beta}_{1} + c^{-1} \widehat{\beta}_{2} \times c x_{i} = \widehat{\beta}_{1} + \widehat{\beta}_{2}x_{i} = \widehat{y}_{i}^{(1)}.
\] If the models generate the same fitted values, they also generate the same residuals. Thus since the SSR and SST is the same for both models, their \(R^{2}\) values should also be the same.







During the course, we often consider the situation of correct specification, i.e. the data-generation process and the model coincide. Let us consider a situation in which this is not true. Suppose the data-generation process is given by \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i},
\] whereas the model that we estimate is the no-intercept model \[
y_{i} = \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i}.
\] Is the least-squares estimator of \(\beta_{2}\) in our model unbiased for the true value of \(\beta_{2}\) in the data-generation process?






CautionSolution





The estimator of the slope coefficient based on the no-intercept model is given by \[
\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}.
\] However, the data is generated according to \(y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i}\). Plugging this into the estimator yields \[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\beta}_{2} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} \\
                    &= \beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} + \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\] We proceed to take expectations: \[
\begin{aligned}
E(\widehat{\beta}_{2}) &= E \left(\beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} + \beta_{2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} \right) \\
&= \beta_{2} + \beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}E(u_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}} \\
&= \beta_{2} + \beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}},
\end{aligned}
\] where we used that \(x_{i}\) is nonrandom by Assumption 2.2 and \(E(u_{i}) = 0\) by Assumption 2.3. Thus, \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\) is biased and the bias equals \(\beta_{1} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}}\)

title: Week 6 - Exercises
text:
Exercise 2
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be two random variables.

In the law of total expectation (or alternatively, law of iterated expectations), we write \(E(x) = E(E(x|y))\). The inner expectation is taken with respect to the conditional distribution \(x|y\). With respect to which distribution is the outer expectation taken?
Let \(x\) be binomially distributed with parameters \(n\) and \(y\), where \(y\) follows a uniform distribution \(U(0,1)\). Compute \(E(x)\).







CautionSolution






The outer expectation is with respect to the marginal distribution of \(Y\).
Suppose \(x \sim Bin(n, y)\), with \(y \sim U(0,1)\). Then, according to the law of total expectation, \(E(x) = E(E(x|y))\). We can compute \(E(x|y) = ny\), as conditional on \(y\), we have a binomial distribution with fixed parameters \(n\) and \(y\). Now, the outer expectation is \(E(ny)\), which we can compute using information on the marginal distribution of \(y\). Namely, \(E(y) = 1/2\), as \(y\) is uniformly distributed with bounds \(0\) and \(1\). Thus, \(E(x) = E(E(x|y)) = E(ny) = n E(y) = n/2\).

title: Week 6 - Exercises
text:
Exercise 3
Consider the simple linear regression model \[
y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i} + u_{i}.
\]

If \(\Cov(x_{i}, u_{i}) = 0\) and \(E(u_{i}) = 0\), then we have \(E(u_{i}|x_{i}) = 0\). Is this true or false? Explain why or give a (counter-)example.
Suppose \(x_{i}\) is standard normally distributed and \(y_{i} = x_{i}^{2}\). Determine the correlation between \(x_{i}\) and \(y_{i}\).

Hint: Compute the covariance between \(x_{i}\) and \(y_{i}\) and make use of the fact that \(x_{i}\) is normally distributed.

The previous exercise gave some interesting insights. If you did it correctly, you found that the correlation is zero. In the code block below, you find code to simulate some data. For \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), generate \(x_{i} \sim N(\mu = 0, \sigma = 5)\) and take \(y_{i} = x_{i}^{2}\) with \(n = 500\). After that we do the following.

We estimate three different regression models: the intercept-only model, a regression of \(x\) on \(y\), and a regression of \(x^2\) on \(y\).
We create three scatterplots between \(x\) and \(y\) and include the results of the regression models. Moreover, we include a scatterplot between \(x^2\) and \(y\) and include the regression results of the third model.


Explain for plot 1 why \(E(u_{i}|x_{i}) = 0\) is violated, for plot 2 and 3 why the results are not useful, and for plot 4 what insights it gives us.


Click here to see the base R plotting code
# 1. Setup and Data Generation
set.seed(123456)
n  <- 500
x  <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 5)
x2 <- x^2
y  <- x2  # Directly using x2 since y = x^2

# 2. Model Fitting
models <- list(
  lm(y ~ 1),
  lm(y ~ x),
  lm(y ~ x2)
)

# 3. Visualization Configuration
options(repr.plot.width = 5, repr.plot.height = 15)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

# 4. Plotting
# Plot the first three models against (x, y)
for (i in 1:3) {
  plot(x, y, main = paste("Model", i))
  abline(models[[i]], col = "red")
}

# Plot the final quadratic model against (x2, y)
plot(x2, y, main = "Model 3 (Linearized)")
abline(models[[3]], col = "red")















CautionSolution






False. We can show that \(E(u_{i} | x_{i}) = 0\) implies both \(\Cov(x_{i}, u_{i}) = 0\) and \(E(u_{i}) = 0\), but not vice versa. Counterexample: let \(x_{i} \sim N(0,1)\) and let \(u_{i} \sim x_{i}^2 - 1\). Then \(E(u_{i}) = E(x_{i}^{2}) - 1 = 0\) and \(\Cov(x_{i}, u_{i}) = E(x_{i}(x_{i}^{2} - 1)) = E(x_{i}^{3}) - E(x_{i}) = 0\). However, \(E(u_{i} | x_{i}) = x_{i}^{2} - 1 \neq 0\) unless \(x = \pm 1\).
Theoretically, the correlation is zero. Note that \(\Cov(x_{i}, y_{i}) = E(x_{i}y_{i}) - E(x_{i})E(y_{i}) = E(x_{i}^3) - E(x_{i})E(x_{i}^{2}) = 0\) as \(E(x_{i}) = 0\) (zero mean) and \(E(x_{i}^3) = 0\) (symmetry distribution). [In fact, all odd moments of the normal distribution are equal to zero].
Plot 1 show that between -5 and 5, the mean of \(u\) is below \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), while outside that interval the mean of \(u\) is larger than \(\widehat{\beta}_0\). Thus, clearly we do not have \(E(u_{i}|x_{i}) = 0\) for all \(x_{i}\). Plot 2 and 3 demonstrate that the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is simply not linear. In plot 3, we try to be clever and make use of the model that tries to link \(y\) to \(x^2\), but this cannot be displayed as a linear relation in the plot of \(x\) and \(y\). Plot 4 displays that a linear regression model could work perfectly well, but only if it is between \(x^{2}\) and \(y\), and not \(x\) and \(y\). That means that we would actually estimate \(y_{i} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_{i}^{2} + u_{i}\), which is a perfectly valid linear regression model! [Note that the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is nonlinear, but it can be captured in a linear regression model, as the variables are allowed to be transformed. The model needs to be linear in its parameters].

title: Week 6 - Exercises
text:
Exercise 4

Suppose \((x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n})\) are independent and identically distributed, each with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^{2}\). In the following derivations, indicate at which equality sign(s) we use the properties (i) independence, (ii) identical distribution, (iii) linearity property of the mean or (iv) scaling property of the variance.


\(E(\overline{x}) = E(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}) = \frac{1}{n} E(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} E(x_{i}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mu = \frac{1}{n} n\mu = \mu\).
\(\Var(\overline{x}) = \Var(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i})  = \frac{1}{n^2} \Var(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Var(x_{i}) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma^{2} = \frac{1}{n^2} n\sigma^{2} = \sigma^{2}/n\).


Decide which assumption, (i) independence and/or (ii) identical distribution is most likely violated in the following examples.


Researchers want to investigate the effect of class attendance on grades for econometrics students at the VU. The researchers come to a class of Econometrics I and ask all students to fill out a questionnaire. The researchers leave the room and pick the questionnaires up 10 minutes later.
Researchers want to investigate the effect of class attendance on grades for econometrics students at the VU. The researchers come to a lecture of Introduction of Programming. The researchers randomly pick some students in the lecture to fill out the questionnaires and stay in the room to pick them up 10 minutes later.







CautionSolution






Let’s consider every equality sign for the two derivations just for the sake of completeness.


Definition \(\overline{x}\) (first equality), linearity expectation (second and third equality), identical distribution (fourth equality), simple algebra (fifth and sixth equality). [Note: independence is actually not needed for unbiasedness of the sample mean].
Definition \(\overline{x}\) (first equality), scaling property of the variance (second equality), independence (third equality), idential distribution (fourth equality), simple algebra (fifth and sixth equality). [Note: variance of sum is sum of variances under independence, which can be seen as there are no covariances].


See below.


A sample is taken from the same population (econometrics students), so identically distribution assumption is probably fine. However, independence is most likely violated, as the students in the classroom share a peer environment (e.g. work together a lot - maybe even when filling in the questionnaire). Thus, it is likely not a random sample. [Note: another clever argument could be that the students in Econometrics I overrepresent second-year students, while the researchers are interested in “econometrics students” as a whole. It does not directly violate the i.i.d.-ness assumption, but the sample might not be representative for the population].
The sample might not be takes from the same population, as there are not only econometrics students in the class but also business analytics and mathematics students. Thus, the respondents probably do not have identical distributions. By randomly picking students in the classroom, the researchers have tried to rule out dependence the best way possible.

title: Week 6 - Exercises
text:
Exercise 5
Consider the following proof sketch of unbiasedness of \(\widehat{\beta}_{2}\) under correct specification, i.e. both the DGP and model is given by \(y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_{i} + u_{i}\).

The least-squares estimator of \(\beta_{2}\) is given by \(\widehat{\beta}_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})^{2}}\).
Plugging in \(y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_{2} x_i + u_i\) and \(\overline{y} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \overline{x} + \overline{u}\) yields \(\widehat{\beta}_2 = \beta_2 + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})^{2}}\) because \(\overline{u} = 0\).
Now, \(E(\widehat{\beta}_2) = \beta_{2}\) only if \(E \left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})^{2}} \right) = 0\).
We know that \(E \left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})u_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \overline{x})^{2}} \right) = \frac{E(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i})}{E\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}}\), so we have to show that the numerator equals zero.
Using the law of total expectation: \(E(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})u_{i}) = E_{x_{i}}[\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x})E_{u_i | x_{i}}(u_{i} | x_{i})] = E_{x_{i}}[\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - \overline{x}) \times 0] = 0\).

The proof sketch above contains some mistakes. Find them and explain why they are mistakes. Afterwards, fix them to make the proof sketch correct. Complete the sketch by indicating what assumptions are used (and where exactly).






CautionSolution





The mistakes and used assumptions are as follows:

In point b., we don’t get the expression due to \(\overline{u} = 0\), but because \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})\overline{u} = \overline{u} (n\overline{x} - n\overline{x}) = \overline{u} \times 0 = 0\). Note that generally \(\overline{u} \neq 0\).
In point d., we cannot claim that the expectation of a fraction is the fraction of the expectations (!). One can find easy counterexamples (even under independence of random variables) and a formal proof can be made using Jensen’s Inequality. In general, \(E(1/y) \geq 1/E(y)\) because the function \(f(y) = 1/y\) is convex for \(y > 0\).
In point d., it also does not hold that we have to show that “the numerator equals zero” (because the first part is not true). The complete fraction needs to be zero in expectation.
In point e., the conditioning is wrong. In order to pull \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})\) out of the inner expectation, we need to condition on all \(x\), i.e. \(X = (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\). It is insufficient to condition on just one \(x_{i}\), as e.g. \(\overline{x}\) consists of all \(x\).
In point e., we therefore use \(E(u_{i} | x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}) = E(u_{i} | x_{i}) = 0\), where the first equality is due random sampling where respondents \(i\) and \(j\) are independent for \(i \neq j\)). The second equality follows by strict exogeneity. Note that the outer expectation, which is applied to the whole fraction, is with respect to the distribution of \(X = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})\), and should thus be denoted \(E_{X}\) instead of \(E_{x_{i}}\).

title: Week 1 - Approximation
text:
Contents
Note that we consider a simplified setting first. That is, we do not yet deal with random events and in fact, we answer the following (simple) question: given a collection of points, how can we draw the best line through them? Thus, we are dealing with a problem of approximation rather than estimation. Two methods that define distance differently are studied: least squares and least absolute deviations. To assess how well the line fits the points in the graph, we study measures of fit. Lastly, we study how the fit is affected whenever we add or omit variables.

title: Week 1 - Approximation
text:
A simplified setting
Before we define the linear regression model in its typical form, we take a step back by assuming that nothing is uncertain. That is, we have \(n\) points \((x_{i}, y_{i})\) but these should not be seen as outcomes of a random process. An example with \(n=100\) points can be found in Figure 1(a). You should view the problem as someone drawing \(n\) points on a piece of paper and then asking you: what is the best-fitting line through all these points? This is a problem of approximation instead of estimation. The difference might not be clear to you just yet, but throughout discussing Chapter 1 and 2 of ITE you should get an intuition why this distinction matters.



Figure 1a shows a scatter plot with \(n=100\) points. Figure 1b shows possible best-fitting lines.


From looking at Figure 1a, we can imagine that if a so-called “best-fitting line” exists, that it is probably upward-sloping as higher values of \(x\) are typically also accompanied with higher values of \(y\). But how should the “best-fitting line” look like? Figure 1b shows three plausible candidates depicted in blue, red and purple. They reveal that it is complicated to determine a “best-fitting line” with the naked eye. In order to find such a line, we have to model the problem mathematically and define an objective function specifying what “best fit” actually means.

title: Week 1 - Approximation
text:
Mathematical representation
If all points were located on a line, we could represent every point by \(y= a + bx\), where \(a\) denotes the intercept and \(b\) the slope. However, since the points are scattered around, we need something extra. That is, we can define every point \((x_{i},y_{i})\) as \[
y_{i} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_{i} + u_{i}, \qquad (i = 1, \ldots, n),
\tag{1}\] where the \(u_{i}\) are vertical deviations from the line and \(n\) denotes the number of observations. The only reason that we replaced our \(a\) and \(b\) by \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) is because we need more \(\beta\)s when we generalize the problem. In other words, it is just a notational convenience as you will find out soon.
Now that we have modelled every point \((x_{i},y_{i})\) for \(i = 1,\ldots, n\), we have to think about what properties the best-fitting line should have. Intuitively, the line should probably lie close to the points. It is impossible to lie near all the points, but overall, it should probably go somewhat “through the middle of the cloud of dots”. We need to formalize this notion mathematically:






NoteDistance



Choose \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) in such a way that the distance from the line to the observations is as small as possible (or equivalently, make the deviations as small as possible).


The previous quote is still not formal enough, because we need to define distance. If we were to add up all the \(u_{i}\) values, we would also include negative values in our distance measure, which does not seem right. There are various ways to define distance, but we consider the following function \[
\phi(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_{i}^{2} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \beta_{1} - \beta_{2} x_{i})^{2},
\tag{2}\] and minimize this function with respect to \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\).
We can see that our original problem can be formulated as an optimization problem. Because there is no randomness involved (remember: all points \((x,y)\) are simply fixed), we call the solution to the minimization problem the least squares approximator (so not estimator!).






Tip📚 Read in ITE



What we did so far is very close to Section 1.1 and 1.2 of ITE, so you might want to have a look at those sections before we continue.
We are now going to derive the least squares approximator using results from calculus that you are familiar with (not included in the book). Afterwards, we continue in ITE where we use vector and matrix to derive the same result and generalize to more variables.

title: Week 1 - Approximation
text:
Deriving the least-squares approximator
We can minimize the function \(\phi(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})\) by taking partial derivatives of \(\phi(\beta)\) with respect to \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\), setting them equal to zero and solving the system of equations.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \phi(\beta_1,\beta_2)}{\partial \beta_1}
&=
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial (y_i - \beta_1 - \beta_2 x_i )^{2}}{\partial \beta_1} \notag \\
&=
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial ( y_i - \beta_1 - \beta_2 x_i )^{2}}{\partial (y_i - \beta_1 - \beta_2 x_i )} \;
\frac{\partial (y_i - \beta_1 - \beta_2 x_i )}{\partial \beta_1} \notag \\
& =  \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2 (y_i - \beta_1 - \beta_2 x_i) \times (-1) \notag \\
& =  -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \beta_1 - \beta_2 x_i).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\] It is a good exercise to check that the second partial derivative is given by \[
\frac{\partial \phi(\beta_1,\beta_2)}{\partial \beta_2} =  -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i}y_{i} - \beta_{1}x_{i} - \beta_{2}x_{i}^{2}).
\tag{4}\] The optimal \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) are the values for which (3) and (4) are equal to zero. These are called the first-order conditions.
We continue by setting both equations equal to zero and multiplying them by \(-\frac{1}{2n}\). In addition, we multiply (3) by \(\overline{x}\) to obtain: \[
\overline{x} \ \overline{y} - \beta_{1} \overline{x} - \beta_{2}\overline{x}^{2} = 0,
\tag{5}\] \[
\overline{xy} - \beta_{1} \overline{x} - \beta_{2} \overline{x^2} = 0,
\tag{6}\] where \(\overline{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\) and \(\overline{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i}\) represent the sample mean of \(x\) and \(y\), respectively, \(\overline{xy} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i}\) is the sample mean of the variable \(xy\) and \(\overline{x^{2}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}\) is the sample mean corresponding to the variable \(x^{2}\).






WarningBe careful!



Note that generally \(\overline{xy} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} \neq \overline{x} \ \overline{y}\) and similarly, \(\overline{x}^{2} \neq \overline{x^{2}}\).
Not convinced? Try out a simple numerical example and you will see it!


Subtracting (5) from (6) results in \[
[\overline{xy} - \overline{x} \ \overline{y}] - \beta_{2}[\overline{x^2} - \overline{x}^{2}] = 0,
\] from which we can find the least-squares approximator \[
b_{2} = \frac{\overline{xy} - \overline{x} \ \overline{y}}{\overline{x^2} - \overline{x}^{2}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}y_{i} - \overline{x} \ \overline{y}}{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2} - \overline{x}^{2}}.
\tag{7}\] Given \(b_{2}\), we can easily find an expression for \(b_{1}\), as setting (3) equal to zero, multiplying it by \(-\frac{1}{2n}\) and evaluating it at the optimal solution yields the relation \[
\overline{y} - b_{1} - b_{2}\overline{x} = 0 \implies b_{1} = \overline{y} - b_{2}\overline{x}.
\]






WarningLeast squares derivation



Any econometrician should know how to derive the least squares estimator in the simple linear model. The derivations on this page are kept short. It is a good exercise to do the derivations by yourself step-by-step.


Whereas the expression for \(b_{2}\) in (7) is of course perfectly valid, the estimator for the slope coefficient is often presented in the following way \[
b_{2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})(y_{i} - \overline{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \overline{x})^{2}} = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_{x}^{2}} = r_{xy} \frac{s_{y}}{s_{x}},
\tag{8}\] because it clearly shows that \(b_{2}\) can be represented in terms of the sample covariance (\(s_{xy}\)) and sample correlation (\(r_{xy}\)) between \(x\) and \(y\) as well as the sample variance of \(x\) (\(s^{2}_{x}\)) and sample variance of \(y\) (\(s^{2}_{y}\)). Even though we are dealing with two equal expressions for \(b_{2}\), it is important that you can show the result in two directions: i.e, going from (7) as starting point to (8) and vice versa (from 8 to 7). We leave these derivations as one of the exercises.

Residuals and fitted values
Now that we have found the least-squares approximation, we can define some useful terms. Make sure that you do not mix them up. Previously, we defined the deviations \(u_{i}\), which we can also present in the following way \[
u_{i} = y_{i} - \beta_{1} - \beta_{2}x = y_{i} - (\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{i}), \qquad (i = 1,\ldots, n).
\] In other words, a deviation \(u_{i}\) is the difference between the point \(y_{i}\) and the line \(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}x\). Because the \(\beta\)s are unknown to us, this represents the true line. We can approximate this true line by replacing the \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) by the least-squares approximators that we just derived. This way, we get \[
e_{i} = y_{i} - b_{1} - b_{2}x = y_{i} - (b_{1} + b_{2}x_{i}), \qquad (i = 1,\ldots, n),
\] where \(e_{i}\) is called a residual. The residual can thus be seen as “the part that remains” after approximating the line and subtracting it from \(y_{i}\). Thus, do not forget: the deviation \(u_{i}\) is formed based on the true parameters \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\), while the residual is based on the approximated parameters \(b_{1}\) and \(b_{2}\). Even though this might only seem a subtle difference, it is crucial in understanding linear regression.
After defining residuals, we can revisit the first-order conditions that we obtained by setting (3) and (4) equal to zero. Since these two equations hold for any admissible combination of (\(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\)), they also hold when evaluated at the optimal solution (\(b_{1},b_{2}\)). They lead to the following two conditions holding true: \[
\text{F.O.C. 1: } \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i} = 0, \qquad \text{F.O.C. 2: } \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i}x_{i} = 0,
\] which means that the residuals are orthogonal to the intercept (F.O.C. 1) and to the regressor \(x\) (F.O.C. 2). At this point, it is important to understand that least squares imposes these conditions.
Besides the residuals, we can also define fitted values or the predictor as \[
\hat{y}_{i} = b_{1} + b_{2}x_{i}, \qquad (i = 1,\ldots, n),
\] because for a given value of \(x_{i}\), this is what the line ‘predicts’ the value of \(y_{i}\) to be. The difference between \(y_{i}\) and \(\hat{y}_{i}\) is, as we saw before, the residual \(e_{i}\).


Generalizing these results
Deriving the least-squares approximator is rather straightforward when we have only one variable \(x\), because the problem boils down to solving a system of two unknowns (\(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\)). If we have \(k\) parameters to estimate, then we would have to take \(k\) partial derivates, set them equal to zero, and continue to solve the system of equations. We can circumvent this problem using vector and matrix calculus.






Tip📚 Read in ITE



Read Section 1.3 - 1.7.
These sections focus on the same derivations that we have done so far, but then based on multiple variables. In short:

Section 1.3 shows how to derive the least-squares approximation by writing (1) in matrix form. In fact, the found solution \(b = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\) is shown not to depend on the number of variables contained in \(X\).
Section 1.4 consists of an alternative derivation, but one needs to know the solution of the optimization problem in advance for this proof to work.
Section 1.5 defines residuals and discusses their main properties.
Section 1.6 provides a geometric interpretation of least squares and the first-order conditions.
Section 1.7 discusses an alternative method Least Absolute Deviations (LAD) to approximate the parameteres and makes the comparison with least squares.

title: Week 1 - Approximation
text:
The fit
We determined how to approximate the parameters in the model, but this does not tell us whether the approximation is ‘good’. We are going to define two measures of fit to make such a judgement. But first, we will introduce three important quantities: \[
\text{Total sum of squares: } \quad \text{SST} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} = y'Ay,
\tag{9}\] \[
\text{Sum of squared residuals: } \quad \text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i}^{2} = e'e,
\tag{10}\] \[
\text{Explained sum of squared: } \quad \text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_{i} - \overline{y})^{2} = \hat{y}'A\hat{y},
\tag{11}\] where (9) represents the total variation in the dependent variable \(y\), (10) the total unexplained variation in \(y\) and (11) the total variation in the predicted value \(\hat{y}\). Note that all sums are build up in a similar way as a sample variance by considering the variable minus its sample mean. This is clearly seen in the definition of SST. The other two need some further inspection. As exercises, we will show that \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i} = 0\) generally and that \(\overline{y} = \overline{\hat{y}}\). This explains why SSR and SSE are defined “differently”.
Based on the definitions above, we can now introduce the coefficient of determination or often just called R squared: \[
R^{2} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}.
\] Provided there is a constant term among the regressors, the value of \(R^{2}\) lies in the interval \([0,1]\) and can therefore be interpreted as the percentage of variation in the dependent variable explained by the independent variables. Its popularity stems from this easy interpretation.
Another measure of fit that is often reported is the standard error of the regression (SER) and is defined as \[
\text{SER } = \sqrt{\frac{\text{SSR}}{n-k}},
\] where \(k\) denotes the number of regressors (number of columns in \(X\)). It approximates the standard deviation of \(u\) (denoted by \(\sigma_{u}\)) and can thus be compared to the sample standard deviation of \(y\) (denoted by \(s_{y}\)). If the value of the SER is low compared to \(s_{y}\) it indicates that the model explains a lot of the variation in the dependent variable \(y\).






Tip📚 Read in ITE



Read Section 1.8 and 1.9.

Section 1.8 shows how to derive \(R^{2}\) using SST, SSR, SSE and the matrix \(A\) and the importance of the first-order conditions.
Section 1.9 centers around the questions How many variables should we include in the model? And which ones should we pick?. This is important for model selection, a key issue in econometrics.
