This week’s contents
The website does not really offer new material this week. Instead, it helps you to understand the proofs of finding the best linear unbiased estimator and the best linear predictor in the context of the linear regression model. The main challenge lies in understanding the proving strategy, which is quite different from what you are typically used to. The remaining sections in the book (Section 2.14 - 2.18) focus on the difficult task of model selection. What are important considerations for including or excluding variables from your model?

title: Week 3 - Best unbiased estimation and prediction
text:
Best unbiased estimation
To find the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of \(\beta\), we proceed as follows. We first solve a simpler problem, which consists of finding the BLUE of \(w'\beta\), i.e., a linear combination of \(\beta\) as \(w\) is a \(k \times 1\) vector. In fact, we did this last week already. This problem is relatively straightforward to solve, because the objective function is scalar-valued in this case. Next, we are going to use the optimal solution found for this problem as an educated guess for the BLUE of \(\beta\) (or even more general, \(W'\beta\)), where \(W\) is now a \(k \times m\) matrix. Because the objective function would be matrix-valued in this case, we cannot rely on standard calculus and a different proving style is required.

Linear combination of \(\beta\)
Last week, we considered the estimation of a linear combination of the \(\beta\)s. That is, \[
\theta = w'\beta = w_{1}\beta_{1} + \cdots + w_{k}\beta_{k}.
\] We assume that the model coincides with the DGP, and Assumptions 2.1-2.3 hold. Then we took the following strategy:

We consider a linear estimator of the data, given by \(\widehat{\theta} = a'y\), where the \(n \times 1\) vector \(a\) is to be chosen optimally.
We want the estimator to be unbiased, i.e., \(E(\widehat{\theta}) = \theta\), which implies \(X'a = w\).
We want to have the lowest variance possible, thus we want to minimize \(\Var(\widehat{\theta}) = \sigma^{2}a'a\) (which is once again a scalar, as it equals \(\sigma^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}\)).

To find the BLUE, we solved a constrained minimization problem which is defined by the following strictly convex Lagrangian function \[
\psi (a) = a'a/2 - l'(X'a - w),
\] where \(l\) is a \(k \times 1\) vector of Lagrangian multipliers. Because the objective function is scalar-valued, standard calculus could be used to find the optimal solution \(\widehat{\theta} = a'y = w'(X'X)^{-1}X'y\).






NoteSome examples



Let \(\beta = (\beta_{1}, \ldots, \beta_{k})'\) and consider the following examples:

\(w' = (0, 1, \ldots, 0)\) gives \(w'\beta = \beta_{2}\).
\(w' = (1, -1, \ldots, 0)\) gives \(w'\beta = \beta_{1} - \beta_{2}\).
\(w' = (3, 2, \ldots, 0)\) gives \(w'\beta = 3\beta_{1} + 2\beta_{2}\).

Note that \(w'\beta\) always reduces to a scalar in this setting.




Estimation of \(\beta\)
Note that the steps in this scenario are very similar at first, it is just the dimensions of the objects that differ. That is, the problem reduces to

We consider a linear estimator of the data, given by \(\widehat{\theta} = A'y\), where \(A\) is an \(n \times m\) matrix to be chosen optimally.
We want the estimator to be unbiased, i.e., \(E(\widehat{\theta}) = \theta\), which implies \(X'A = W\).
We want to have the lowest variance possible, thus we want to minimize \(\Var(\widehat{\theta}) = \sigma^{2}A'A\) (which is an \(m \times m\) matrix).

Even though the problem appears analogous to the previous one, the crucial difference lies in the fact that we are now dealing with matrix functions. Calculus and Lagrangian theory are not applicable in this case. The proving strategy works as follows:

For \(\widehat{\theta} = a'y\), we found that \(a = X(X'X)^{-1}w\) constitutes the optimal weight.
We now make the following educated guess. For \(\widehat{\theta} = A'y\), we expect that \(A = X(X'X)^{-1}W\).
We proceed by defining \(D = A - X(X'X)^{-1}W\) and aim at showing \(D = 0\) at the optimal solution.







NoteMultiple linear combinations



Note that \(W'\beta\) generally results in an \(m \times 1\) vector, which contains \(m\) linear combinations of \(\beta\).
One of the most interesting cases is \(W'= I_{k}\), in which \(W'\beta = \beta\). That is, we consider \(m = k\) trivial linear combinations because the matrix \(W'\) essentially consists of \(k\) standard basis vectors (i.e., a vector \(e_{i}\) which has zero at every displacement \(j \neq i\) and one at displacement \(i\)).








Tip📚 Read in ITE



Now that the intuition behind the proving techniques has been discussed, you are ready to read

Section 2.10, which is a proof of the Gauss-Markov theorem.
Section 2.11, which highlights a crucial difference between \(u\) and \(e\), characterized by their respective variance matrices.
Section 2.12, in which we construct a quadratic estimator for \(\sigma^{2}\) with the property of being unbiased.

For the last section, it is advisable to refresh your knowledge about square matrices (Section A.1), the trace of a matrix (Section A.2), properties of positive definite matrices (Section A.5) and the matrix \(M\) (Section A.8).

title: Week 3 - Best unbiased estimation and prediction
text:
Prediction
In the topic prediction, we use very similar arguments as in best unbiased estimation to derive the best linear predictor. The setup is as follows:

We have estimated the linear model \(y = X\beta + u\) based on a set of observations \((y, X)\), where \(y\) is an \(n \times 1\) vector and \(X\) an \(n \times k\) matrix of regressors.
Now we still have other data, \((y_{*}, X_{*})\), at our disposal, where \(y_{*}\) is an \(m \times 1\) vector and \(X_{*}\) is an \(m \times k\) matrix.
We assume that this data comes from the same DGP as \((y, X)\) and we use it to answer the question: how well does our predict the corresponding value of the dependent variable?.
To do this, we assume the same standard linear regression model is also valid for the new observations: \[
y_{*} = X_{*}\beta + u_{*},
\] where \(u_{*}\) has zero mean, variance \(\sigma^{2}I_{m}\), and is uncorrelated with \(u\). In other words, the same assumptions hold for this ‘new’ model.







NoteInterpretation



You can interpret this procedure as follows. If we want to evaluate how well our model does at prediction, it is arguably strange to first use the data \((y, X)\) to estimate \(\beta\) and to afterwards use exactly the same data \((y, X)\) to make predictions. Ideally, you want to see whether the estimated model generalizes well to data that we have not yet seen.
This is exactly what we are doing here. We use one data set \((y, X)\) to estimate the unknown parameter vector \(\beta\). Afterwards, we use a separate data set \((y_{*}, X_{*})\) to evaluate the predictive performance of our model.


As can be read in ITE, there are two ways to approach the prediction problem, and they have quite different mathematical implications. Suppose we have a predictor \(\hat{y}_{*}\) than we could compare this predicted value with:

The expected value \(E(y_{*}) = X_{*}\beta\). This is the easier case, because this is a nonrandom quantity. It can be argued that this is again an estimation problem rather than a prediction problem. In fact, by defining \(X_{*} = W'\), this problem can be posed as showing that \(W'\widehat{\beta}\) is the best linear unbiased estimator of \(W'\beta\). Note that this is exactly what we did for best unbiased estimation. Thus, Proposition 2.2 directly applies.
The true realization \(y_{*}\). This is a bit more complicated. Note that \(y_{*} = X_{*}\beta + u_{*}\) is a random vector due to \(u_{*}\) being part of it. We are now in the prediction framework. To find the best linear predictor, we have to proceed as follows:


Define the prediction error \(\widehat{y}_{*} - y_{*}\) and ensure that it is zero in expectation (unbiased). In other words, on average, we are not systematically predicting a value that is too high or too low.
The variance of the prediction error should be as small as possible.

The proving style is once again very similar. Our educated guess is that \(\widehat{y}_{*} = X_{*}\widehat{\beta} = X_{*}(X'X)^{-1}X'y\) is the best linear predictor. Therefore, we define \(D = A - X(X'X)^{-1}X_{*}'\) as the difference between the weights of any other linear predictor of \(y_{*}\) and our educated guess. If the predictor is unbiased and the prediction error variance is minimized, we hope to find \(D = 0\). That is, the optimal weights are indeed \(A = X(X'X)^{-1}X_{*}'\).






Tip📚 Read in ITE



With the explanation above in mind, you are ready to read

Section 2.13, which derives the best linear predictor.

Note that it is crucial this week that you understand the difference between quantities being random and nonrandom. If you have difficulties with that, it is highly advisable to revisit these concepts.

title: Week 3 - Best unbiased estimation and prediction
text:
A difficult task: model selection
Many textbooks on introductory econometrics start by considering the linear regression model under correct specification. This means that the model that is being estimated coincides with the truth, i.e. the data-generation process (DGP). Whereas this setup is extremely convenient to evaluate the performance of the model, it is unfortunately a rather unrealistic one in practice. In real life, the DGP is almost never known to the practitioner. However, this does not mean that we should give up our challenge of evaluating our model’s performance.
Instead of assuming that our chosen model exactly coincides with the truth, econometricians often also take another approach. They consider two different model specifications and compare these two to each other. This gives rise to the following: \[
y = X\beta + u = X_{1}\beta_{1} + X_{2}\beta_{2} + u,
\] with \(X = (X_{1} : X_{2})\) is called the unrestricted model, and \[
y = X_{1}\beta_{1} + u_{1},
\] is called the restricted model, where the restriction is given by \(\beta_{2} = 0\). For clarification, note that \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) are two subvectors of \(\beta\). That is, for \(k = k_{1} + k_{2}\), the \(k \times 1\) vector \(\beta\) can be written as \(\beta = (\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})'\), where \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) are of order \(k_{1} \times 1\) and \(k_{2} \times 1\), respectively. If we assume the DGP coincides with the unrestricted model, we can investigate the effects of ‘underspecifying’ our model.






NoteExample



One of the simplest examples is the following. Suppose that we are given the simple linear regression model \[
y = \beta_{1}\imath + \beta_{2}x + u,
\] written in vector notation, as the unrestricted model. In this case, \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{2}\) are scalars! The restricted model is given by the no-intercept model \[
y = \beta_{2}x + u_{1}.
\] We could now investigate the properties of the least-squares estimator \(\widehat{\beta}_{2r}\) in the restricted model. In fact, if the constant term in the DGP is nonzero, this estimator will not perform well. Generally, it is biased and inconsistent.


In the following, we briefly consider the main take-away message from the remaining sections of Chapter 2 in ITE.

Bias-variance trade-off
Section 2.15 and 2.16 focus on a very important concept in econometrics and data science: the bias-variance trade-off. Ideally, we want to have both the bias and variance low, but this is rarely possible simultaneously. Getting unbiased estimates often requires including many regressors in the model. However, the inclusion of many variables requires the estimation of the same large amount of unknown coefficients. This, in turn, increases the variance of the estimator a lot. Conversely, excluding relevant regressors biases the estimation of the coefficients of the variables that are actually included in the model. Thus, the variance of the estimator might be low, but the coefficients are biased.
Both examples highlight the trade-off that needs to be made. In the first case, we might be willing to accept a bit of bias if it goes hand in hand with a substantial reduction in variance. In the second case, we could accept some more variance if the bias gets reduced sufficiently. But what exactly is sufficient?
This is where the mean squared error (MSE) comes in. Following Section B.2 in ITE, we can express the MSE in terms of bias and variance. In the univariate case, we can write \[
\text{MSE}(\widehat{\theta}) = \Var(\widehat{\theta}) + \left(\text{bias}(\widehat{\theta})\right)^{2},
\] while the multivariate case reduces to \[
\text{MSE}(\widehat{\theta}) = \Var(\widehat{\theta}) + \text{bias}(\widehat{\theta})\text{bias}(\widehat{\theta})'.
\] In a way, the MSE embodies the bias-variance trade-off and this makes it a popular measure in econometrics and data science. Choosing between unbiased estimators is relatively simple: you pick the one with the lowest variance. The MSE however also makes the comparison between biased and unbiased estimators possible.


Significance and importance
Whereas the MSE is a measure to compare estimators, it does not directly answer the question which regressors to include in the model and which ones not. Suppose we know the truth. Then we could potentially choose to set up a model that coincides exactly with the truth. The previous discussion on the bias-variance trade-off highlights that we very likely should still opt against it. The difference between significance and importance is important here. Linguisitically, these terms are often used interchangeably, but statistically they have quite distinct meanings.
If a parameter is significant, it simply means that we have enough evidence in the data to credibly argue that its value is different from zero. For a single parameter, we typically establish this by performing a \(t\)-test. We choose a significance level \(\alpha\) in advance (e.g. \(\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.05, 0.1\}\)) and at the chosen significance level, we investigate whether we can reject the null hypothesis that the parameter is zero. In other words, significance is a statistical concept: it says something about how precise we are in estimating an unknown parameter. It does not mean that the parameter is also important.
It could be that you estimate a parameter rather precisely (e.g., because you have a lot of data), you rule it significant based on a \(t\)-test but the parameter is in fact unimportant. Deleting a small, unimportant parameter is generally a good idea because you incur a small bias (the bias depends on the size of the parameter), while much prediction may be gained (the reduction in variance does not depend on the size of the parameter). Thus, it is important that statistical significance is not necessarily decisive for including a variable in the model or not.


Balanced addition
We have argued that, if we know the truth, we can work ourselves towards unbiasedness by including regressors until we reacher the true specification. However, in reality, the truth is generally unknown and adding more regressors to the model does not at all guarantee that the bias decreases. That is why model selection is typically done based on several measures, and in the following chapter we will cover some of these.

Read Section 2.14 - 2.18.
After these sections, you should be convinced that deciding which variables to include in the model is generally not an easy task and several considerations should be made. Make sure that you have a clear picture what happens in the scenario unrestricted model (coinciding with the DGP) versus restricted model, and how it differs when we do not know the truth.

This week’s contents
Last week, we have seen how to perform a \(t\)-test and discusses two important properties of any test, its size and power. Using this knowledge, we can proceed in two ways. First, we are able to set up confidence and prediction intervals. Second, we extend our testing framework to test for restrictions: both for single linear restrictions of the form \(w'\beta = r\) and multiple linear restrictions given by \(R\beta = r\). As special cases of the latter, we will discuss the overall \(F\)-test and the partial \(F\)-test. The final sections of this chapter are, similarly to last chapter, devoted to model selection. We discuss the adjusted \(R^{2}\) as a measure to compare the unrestricted and restricted model, and derive relations with \(s^{2}\) and the \(F\)-statistic. Instead of selecting one model, we discuss the possibility of using multiple models. These last parts are exclusive to the book and won’t be discussed here.

title: Week 5 - Inference (cont’d)
text:
Confidence and prediction intervals
Last week we derived that \[
t_{j} = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j} - \beta_{j}}{\sqrt{s^{2}v_{jj}}} \sim t(n-k),
\tag{1}\] which we can use to perform \(t\)-tests on individual coefficients in the linear regression model. Performing such a test typically gives us a binary choice: either we reject or we fail to reject the null hypothesis. A test and a confidence interval are closely related, but it could be argued that a confidence interval provides the econometrician with more information. We can exploit the fact that for a given \(n\) and \(k\), the distribution of (1) is fully known. Using the steps in the book, we can go from a probability statement to an interval \[
\left( \widehat{\beta}_{j} + c_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{s^{2}v_{jj}}, \widehat{\beta}_{j} + c_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{s^{2}v_{jj}}  \right),
\tag{2}\] where \(c_{\alpha/2}\) and \(c_{1-\alpha/2}\) are the critical values of the \(t(n-k)\) distribution at \(\alpha/2\) and \(1 - \alpha/2\). This provides the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval (if \(\alpha\) expressed in decimals) or \(100 - \alpha\) confidence interval (if \(\alpha\) expressed in percentage) for \(\beta_{j}\). For a symmetric distribution, such as the \(t\)-distribution and the normal distribution, the critical values on both tails only differ by sign. In that case, we can also write \[
\left( \widehat{\beta}_{j} - c_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{s^{2}v_{jj}}, \widehat{\beta}_{j} + c_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{s^{2}v_{jj}}  \right),
\] in which it is understood that \(c_{\alpha/2}\) represents the critical value emerging from the right tail. This latter definition is also often preferred because it already has the plus and minus in the direct definition (in contrast (2) has a plus for both the left and right cut-off because the sign emerges from the critical value). In any case, it shows that it is important to properly define all terms.






NoteExample





If we take \(\alpha = 0.05\), then we obtain the \(100(1-0.05)\% = 95\%\) confidence interval. The critical values are then \(c_{\alpha/2} = c_{0.025}\) and \(c_{1 - \alpha/2} = c_{0.975}\), which ensures that the tails are cut-off at \(2.5\%\) and \(97.5\%\) probability, respectively. Note that we only include \(\alpha\) as a subscript of the critical values, but for the \(t\)-distribution it is also a function of \(n\) and \(k\).
In contrast, consider the case where we could use \[
\frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j} - \beta_{j}}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}v_{jj}}} \sim N(0, 1),
\] for testing, because \(\sigma^{2}\) is known. Note that the critical values for a given \(\alpha\) based on the standard normal distribution \(N(0,1)\), are not functions of \(n\) and \(k\). In other words, replacing \(\sigma^{2}\) by an estimator \(s^{2}\) does not only change the distribution (from normal to \(t\)), but also makes the resulting critical values a function of the remaining degrees of freedom \(n-k\).



Note that the term confidence is very different from probability. Confidence intervals are based on a repeated sampling argument: if we could repeatedly sample from the true process, say \(100\) times, about \(95\) of the resulting intervals capture the true population value \(\beta_{j}\). This is because a confidence interval is actually about a nonrandom quantity \(\beta_{j}\), which lies within certain random bounds with a certain probability. Note that if the hypothesized value does not fall within the confidence interval, then we reject the null hypothesis of a test. Thus, we have a third way of performing a statistical test: (i) compare statistic and critical value, (ii) compare \(p\)-value and significance level, (iii) determine whether the hypothesized value is included in the confidence interval.
We have seen how we can go from estimators and tests to confidence intervals, but we can proceed similarly for prediction intervals. For now, it is important to mention that, even though the naming seems to suggest that confidence and predictio intervals are very similar, they do have striking differences. Confidence intervals considers estimators of a population parameter (such as \(\beta_{j}\)) and uses information of the whole sample. Note that the estimators are essentially determining the random bounds of the interval, because the estimators are functions of the data. Prediction intervals, instead, considers predicting a single data point or multiple data points in a random vector. The source of uncertainty is not just sampling error (i.e., the variation between estimator and population parameter) but also the randomness emerging from the individual data points (i.e., data points are themselves outcomes of random variables). This is a similar discussion as in Week 3, when we compared best linear unbiased estimation and best linear unbiased prediction.

title: Week 5 - Inference (cont’d)
text:
Restricted testing
The \(t\)-test that we considered only allows for testing hypotheses of the form \(\beta_{j} = 0\). Whereas these tests are often employed in empirical work, one might also want to test more complicated hypotheses. Consider the following regression for companies that advertise on Instagram and Tiktok, with the goal to increase sales: \[
\text{Sales}_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} \text{Spending on Instagram}_{i} + \beta_{3} \text{Spending on Tiktok}_{i} + \beta_{4}x_{i,4} + \ldots + \beta_{k}x_{i,k} + u_{i},
\] where \(x_{i,4}\) up to \(x_{i,k}\) are auxiliary variables. The hypothesis \(H_{0}: \beta_{2} + \beta_{3} = 1\) could be interest to managers who want to know whether advertisement spendings on both platforms translate to a one-to-one increase in a company’s sales. This hypothesis only consists of one linear restriction, which can be written in the form \(w'\beta = r\) as \[
w'\beta =
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\beta_{1} \\ \beta_{2} \\ \beta_{3} \\ \vdots \\ \beta_{k}
\end{pmatrix}
= r,
\] with \(r = 1\). One might also test for multiple linear restrictions, which can be represented in the form \(R\beta = r\). The matrix \(R\) is of the order \(m \times k\), where \(m\) represents the number of unique restrictions imposed. This means that \(r\) is now an \(m \times 1\) vector instead of a scalar (which it is in the \(w'\beta = r\) framework).
The test statistics for both scenarios, i.e. \(w'\beta = r\) and \(R\beta = r\), are derived in Section 3.12 and 3.13 respectively. We will not derive the same results here as in the book, but rather focus on how to find the test statistics in case you do not know the expressions by heart. Note that we found the following result last week: \[
\widehat{\beta} \sim N(\beta, \sigma^{2}(X'X)^{-1}).
\] Because linear combinations of normally distributed random variables are also normally distributed, we can easily find \[
w'\widehat{\beta} \sim N(w'\beta, \sigma^{2}w'(X'X)^{-1}w) \quad \text{ and } \quad R\widehat{\beta} \sim N(R\beta, \sigma^{2}R(X'X)^{-1}R').
\] It must be noted that these two results look very similar, but the main difference lies in the fact that \(w'\widehat{\beta}\) follows a univariate normal distribution, while the distribution of \(R\widehat{\beta}\) is multivariate normal.

A single linear restriction
Similar to the derivation of the \(t\)-test, we can first write \[
\frac{w'\widehat{\beta} - w'\beta}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}w'(X'X)^{-1}w}} \sim N(0,1).
\] If \(\sigma^{2}\) was known and imposing under the null hypothesis that \(w'\beta = r\), we could directly use this expression for testing. However, since \(\sigma^{2}\) is generally unknown, we need to replace \(\sigma^{2}\) by \(s^2\). We can proceed almost exactly analogously as for the \(t\)-test of previous week (good exercise for yourself!) to derive \[
t_{w} = \frac{w'\widehat{\beta} - r}{\sqrt{s^{2}w'(X'X)^{-1}w}} \sim t(n-k).
\] Since we have a standard normal distribution, \((n-k)s^{2}/\sigma^{2} \sim \chi^{2}(n-k)\), \(\widehat{\beta}\) and \(s^{2}\) are independent, we can once again use equation B.7 in Section B.4 of Appendix B.

title: Week 5 - Inference (cont’d)
text:
Several linear restrictions
The case for the single linear restriction is relatively straightforward, because all terms are univariate and the steps are similar to last week’s derivation. However, several linear restrictions requires a different approach because the distribution of \(R\widehat{\beta}\) is \(m\)-dimensional. We can rewrite it to a multivariate standard normal distribution, which we denote by \(x\) \[
x = (\sigma^{2}R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1/2}(R\widehat{\beta} - R\beta) \sim N(0,I_{m}).
\tag{3}\] We cannot use this result for hypothesis testing, because \(\sigma^{2}\) is generally unknown and the distribution of \(x\) is multivariate. We cannot perform the same steps as before, because we can only obtain a \(t\)-distribution in case of a univariate normal distribution. Instead, we can convert (3) to another univariate distribution. We can apply equation B.5 to (3) to obtain \[
x'x = \frac{(R\widehat{\beta} - R\beta)'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\widehat{\beta} - R\beta)}{\sigma^{2}} \sim \chi^{2}(m).
\tag{4}\] This helps us to simplify the problem to a univariate distribution. However, we still cannot use this result for hypothesis testing because \(\sigma^{2}\) is unknown.






NoteMatrix functions





The variance matrix of \(R\widehat{\beta}\) is given by \(\sigma^{2}(R(X'X)^{-1}R')\). To obtain (3), we apply a matrix function that gives \(\sigma^{-1}(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1/2}\). Note that, following Section A.6 in Appendix A, we are only allowed to perform this operation whenever the matrix is symmetric and positive definite.
The matrix \(R(X'X)^{-1}R'\) indeed fulfills these conditions. Note that a variance matrix is always symmetric, and \(R(X'X)^{-1}R'\) is positive definite because \(R\) has full row rank \(m\) while the \(k\times k\) matrix \(X'X\) is positive definite and thus invertible due to \(X\) having full column rank \(k\).



We can proceed as follows. Because \(x'x\) in (4) follows a \(\chi^{2}(m)\) distribution, and \((n-k)s^{2}/\sigma^{2} \sim \chi^{2}(n-k)\) with \(\widehat{\beta}\) and \(s^{2}\) independent, we can apply equation B.8 in Section B.4 of Appendix B to convert (4) to the feasible test statistic \[
F_{R} = \frac{(R\widehat{\beta} - r)'(R(X'X)^{-1}R')^{-1}(R\widehat{\beta} - r)/m}{s^{2}} \sim F(m, n-k),
\] under the null hypothesis \(R\beta = r\).

With the explanation above in mind, you are ready to read

Section 3.12 - 3.15.

Note that in Section 3.15, the title contains \(\beta_{2} = 0\). This refers to a \(k_{2} \times 1\) vector \(\beta_{2}\), not a single coefficient in the \(\beta\) vector. That is, we used partitioning to write \(\beta = (\beta_{1}, \beta_{2})'\) where \(\beta_{1}\) is \(k_{1} \times 1\), \(\beta_{2}\) is \(k_{2} \times 1\) and \(\beta\) is \(k \times 1\) with \(k = k_{1} + k_{2}\). The test in Section 3.15 is referred to as the partial F-test.

Section 3.16 - 3.20.

Note that adjusted \(R^{2}\) is a metric for model selection, while \(R^{2}\) is a measure of fit. They serve quite distinct goals. The final sections focus on how selecting between two models enforces a binary choice, which is not always clear-cut. Alternatively, one could think about combining multiple models. We will discuss this in a bit more detail in class.
